The model is studied using the recent observational datasets, including Cosmic Chronometers (CC), Pantheon+SH0ES, and DESI DR2 BAO measurements. While the conventional sampling procedure struggles with slow mixing of parameter chains (τₘₐₓ=1578.3), the neural network, specially trained densely in high likelihood regions, yields converged and highly resolved posterior distributions of the model parameters without significantly compromising the minimum chi-square value. We further discuss the results for physical inferences and also compare the present dark energy model with LambdaCDM statistically using AIC and BIC.

articles.title: Symmetry and Quantum Interference in the Attosecond Domain
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26901v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this review, we examine the interplay of symmetry and quantum interference in the attosecond domain primarily through one- and two-electron photoelectron momentum distributions. Using our own work, we discuss how tailored laser fields provide control over dynamical symmetries, and how quantum-orbit methods make it possible to connect the resulting momentum-space structures to specific ionisation, propagation, and rescattering pathways. Particular emphasis is placed on ultrafast photoelectron holography and nonsequential double ionisation through recollision excitation with subsequent ionisation, where several distinct forms of quantum interference can be identified and manipulated. We also discuss how target properties, including the binding potential, orbital symmetry and parity, modify this mapping. Finally, we consider emerging opportunities offered by non-classical states of light, for which photon statistics and quantum fluctuations provide additional degrees of freedom for controlling symmetry and strong-field electron dynamics.

articles.title: Enhancing analytical photon transport in turbid media through physics-guided neural network corrections
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Analytical methods provide rapid and computationally efficient predictions of light transport in turbid media, making them attractive for real-time and inverse applications. However, their accuracy is limited by the approximations and assumptions used to obtain tractable solutions. On the other hand, Monte Carlo (MC) simulation is widely regarded as the "gold standard" for modeling light transport in turbid media, but its high computational cost limits its use in applications requiring repeated forward evaluations. Here, we introduce a physics-guided residual learning framework that combines the computational efficiency of analytical modeling with the accuracy of MC simulation. As a representative case study, we consider the diffusion approximation (DA), which can exhibit systematic errors under relatively strong absorption, weak scattering, and imperfect boundary treatment. Given the absorption coefficient, scattering coefficient, and anisotropy factor, the corresponding DA prediction is incorporated as a physical prior, while the network learns only the residual between the analytical prediction and the MC reference. Across the evaluated optical-property range, the proposed framework reduces scalar-reflectance RMSE and spatially resolved reflectance RMSLE by factors of approximately 62 and 14, respectively, relative to the diffusion approximation. With only 1% of the available training data, it achieves approximately 87% and 93% lower corresponding errors than a direct neural-network surrogate. These results demonstrate that learning corrections to an analytical physical baseline improves both prediction accuracy and data efficiency.

articles.title: Gerchberg-Saxton Optimized Silicon Metasurface for Sinusoidal Structured-Light Three-Dimensional Imaging
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26956v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) optical imaging based on structured illumination has attracted considerable attention in applications including machine vision, robotics, and computational sensing. However, conventional structured-light systems generally rely on bulky projection components, such as digital micromirror devices and diffractive optical elements, which limit system miniaturization and integration. Here, we demonstrate a compact structured-light 3D imaging platform enabled by a silicon dielectric metasurface operating at a near-infrared wavelength of 940 nm. The desired sinusoidal fringe illumination is encoded into the metasurface through a Gerchberg-Saxton (GS) phase optimization algorithm, which converts the target far-field distribution into a nanoscale phase profile and subsequently into silicon nanopillar geometries. The fabricated metasurface generates high-quality sinusoidal structured illumination, which is integrated with a four-step phase-shifting reconstruction method to recover 3D object profiles. The proposed approach provides a compact and scalable solution for miniaturized structured-light projection and optical 3D sensing.

articles.title: Anchored Exploration in Product Evolution: A Phylogenetic Network Framework for Semiconductor Designs
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26973v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a product phylogenetic network framework for examining anchored exploration. Using 102,465 semiconductor products grouped into 45,996 design families, we distinguish accumulated design continuity (Anchor) from externally precedented feature additions (horizontal transfer, HT). Fitted regressions yield non-monotonic relationships for HT occurrence and descendant carriage, alongside increasing within-family carriage over observed support. These patterns connect technological trajectories and recombination by distinguishing the continuity associated with incorporating external features from that associated with reproducing them in subsequent products.

articles.title: Load-Balanced Neural-Network-Aided Adaptive Tabulation of Phase Equilibria for Transcritical Multiphase Flows
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Simulating high-pressure transcritical flows with phase change is critical for advanced propulsion, yet traditional first-principles approaches, vapor-liquid equilibrium (VLE) calculations, consume most of the runtime and frequently fail to converge. Standalone machine learning models introduce heavy evaluation overhead across large grids, while dynamic tabulation still relies on fragile iterative solvers. To resolve these limitations, this study introduces a hybrid In-Situ Adaptive Tabulation and Artificial Neural Network (ISAT-ANN) framework. A pre-trained ANN replaces the iterative solver during table expansion to guarantee crash-free operation, while ISAT enables rapid data retrieval via local linear interpolation. To eliminate parallel load imbalances, an O(N) greedy load-balancing algorithm redistributes computational tasks across cores. Coupled with Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR), the framework was validated on a Mach 5 shock-droplet interaction benchmark. It accurately captured shock-interface dynamics without instability, achieving a 2.30 times speedup in thermodynamic calculations on a single core and 2.62 times in parallel over standalone ANNs, with AMR providing an additional 2.92 times overall efficiency boost. This plug-and-play framework offers a stable, scalable path for high-fidelity multiphase flow simulations.

articles.title: NeRF-Inspired Neural Fields for 3D Super-resolution of Reacting-Flows
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27284v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The multiscale nature of turbulent reacting flows and the importance of fine-scale structures pose challenges for super-resolution. We investigate a 3D super-resolution framework inspired by Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), called Neural Field Super-Resolution (NFSR), to reconstruct fine-resolution fields from coarsened reacting-flow fields. The proposed formulation adapts the continuous coordinate-conditioned representation of NeRF to physical flow-field reconstruction by conditioning spatial coordinates with local coarse-grid thermochemical information, while eliminating radiance prediction and volume rendering. Principal component analysis is used to provide a compact and low-dimensional representation of the thermochemical state, and a hierarchical extension, H-NFSR, progressively reconstructs the solution through intermediate resolution levels. The framework is evaluated using three-dimensional direct numerical simulation data for a turbulent premixed hydrogen-air flame, with an overall spatial coarsening factor of eight in each coordinate direction. The results demonstrate consistently better prediction measures and a higher ability to reconstruct fine-scale information than tricubic interpolation on the unseen test realization. The hierarchical formulation reduces visible coarse-cell imprinting. In contrast, biased sampling mainly benefits the most localized structures. Three-dimensional isosurface comparisons further show that H-NFSR recovers much of the small and intermediate features of the flow, including surface wrinkling and local flame curvature effects. These results highlight the potential of coordinate-conditioned neural fields as a flexible framework for three-dimensional coarse-to-fine reconstruction of reacting-flow simulations.

articles.title: Machine-learned spectral PDE solvers for fluids and plasmas
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27317v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse regression methods for discovering governing partial differential equations (PDEs) from data are sensitive to observation noise and are not constrained to reproduce the data under forward integration. We address both limitations by performing weak-form discovery in the spatial discretization in which the PDE is solved, learned by differentiating through multistep rollouts anchored at the observed states. The new method, Weak-form Anchored Rollout for PDEs (WARP), produces a machine-learned PDE solver. In this work, we focus on systems amenable to a spectral Galerkin solver. Across eight benchmark fluid and plasma systems, including high-dimensional turbulent simulations, WARP produces numerically stable rollouts from new random initial conditions and substantially improves coefficient recovery, rollout accuracy, and statistical measures compared with a single-step weak-form SINDy baseline.

articles.title: Collective-Variable Stein Variational Gradient Descent for Free Energy Surface Exploration
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27429v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enhanced-sampling methods enable molecular simulations to access configurational regions that are difficult to explore with conventional dynamics, but their efficiency often deteriorates as the number of collective variables (CVs) increases. Here, we introduce an enhanced-sampling framework that couples Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) with parallel restrained molecular dynamics simulations to facilitate exploration of higher-dimensional CV spaces. SVGD collectively transports an ensemble of interacting particles toward a target probability distribution by combining mean forces that guide particles toward low-free-energy regions with kernel-mediated repulsive interactions that maintain particle diversity. We validate the approach using an analytically solvable double-well model, followed by aqueous alanine dipeptide and tripeptide in two- and four-dimensional CV spaces, respectively. In each case, the particle ensemble reproduces the corresponding target distribution, and the reconstructed free-energy surfaces agree closely with analytical or umbrella-sampling references. For alanine dipeptide and tripeptide, CV-SVGD requires substantially less aggregate MD sampling than the corresponding umbrella-sampling reference calculations. These results demonstrate the potential of CV-SVGD as a flexible, parallelizable framework for enhanced sampling in multidimensional CV spaces. We additionally provide an open-source Python implementation to facilitate its adoption.

articles.title: HypoNet Nankai PS: rapid hypocenter determination for the Nankai Trough using physics-informed neural networks with three-dimensional P- and S-wave velocity models
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rapid and accurate hypocenter determination based on three-dimensional (3D) seismic velocity models is essential for seismic monitoring in subduction zones, yet it remains computationally demanding. HypoNet Nankai, a hypocenter determination package that uses physics-informed neural network (PINN) travel-time inference for a realistic 3D P-wave velocity model of the Nankai Trough subduction zone, was designed to address this problem, but supported only P-wave arrival times. Here, we present HypoNet Nankai PS, which extends the framework to both P- and S-wave travel times. We first constructed an S-wave velocity model from the existing P-wave model using empirical conversion relations for marine sediments and the crust. Because the resulting S-wave velocity structure has lower velocities and therefore considerably steeper travel-time gradients, the original PINN training procedure designed for the P-wave velocity structure was insufficient. We therefore revised the training procedure by reconsidering the distribution of collocation points, the NN architecture, and the optimizer. Benchmark comparisons with the fast marching method showed that the revised approach substantially reduced the root-mean-square deviations for both P- and S-waves compared with the original algorithm. Recovery tests using synthetic earthquakes were also performed. When applied to 223 earthquakes recorded by DONET stations off the Kii Peninsula, the system yielded hypocenters generally consistent with the JMA catalog beneath the network, suggesting that the 3D velocity model captures travel-time variations accommodated by JMA's 1D model and station corrections. Farther seaward, the estimated hypocenters were substantially shallower than those in the JMA catalog and were located in the oceanic crust and uppermost mantle, consistent with previous relocations that used DONET data and 3D velocity models.

articles.title: Nanophotonic Extreme Ultraviolet Polarimeter
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27705v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nanophotonic engineering has revolutionized how we manipulate the polarization of visible light. Here, we extend such control to extreme ultraviolet radiation, the spectral region of attosecond science and semiconductor lithography, where transmissive optical elements are lacking. We implement channel waveguides that restrict incident 41-nm-wavelength light to a few modes with defined spatial profiles and propagation constants. By designing the propagation-length-dependent interference of two eigenmodes, we achieve polarization-dependent forward scattering, which we exploit to create a transmissive nanophotonic analyzer that resolves the polarization axis and spectrum of extreme ultraviolet light from a single measurement. With a 0.9deg-sensitivity for polarization rotations in a 1-second measurement and single-shot capability, the device opens new experimental opportunities in ultrafast magneto-optic spectroscopy and at accelerator-based light sources.

articles.title: Searching for Axion Dark Matter via Superconductor-Spin Hybrid Magnetometers
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Axions are a compelling dark matter candidate suggested by theories beyond the Standard Model. The predicted axion-electron coupling and the resulting pseudomagnetic field allow for laboratory axion searches. Here we report an experimental axion search via a superconductor-spin hybrid magnetometer. A state-of-the-art broadband magnetometer with a sensitivity of sub-100 aT/Hz¹/² at tens of kHz has been realized by coupling a ferrite spin sensor to a readout system based on a superconducting quantum interference device. The most stringent terrestrial constraints on the axion-electron coupling have been established in the frequency range 5sim60 kHz. In the future, an improvement on the constraints of more than 4 orders of magnitude is foreseeable through arrays of superconductor-spin hybrid magnetometers with optimized designs. This work demonstrates the potential of superconductor-spin hybrid magnetometers in high-precision magnetic field sensing and the study of fundamental physics.

articles.title: From random patterns to nanophotonic structures: Electromagnetic field prediction without retraining
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27769v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electromagnetic surrogate solvers can accelerate nanophotonic design, but their broader use requires accurate predictions for unseen geometries and material arrangements. Training on random dielectric patterns enables direct prediction of complex electromagnetic fields in diverse two-dimensional nanophotonic structures without retraining. The network takes spatial permittivity distributions as inputs, with training samples drawn from a dataset comprising 700,140 combinations of 5,001 random freeform dielectric patterns and 140 relative permittivities from 2.1 to 16.0. The trained model predicts fields for aperiodic bar arrays, manually defined patterns, inverse-designed metalenses, inverse-designed binary structures, and two-material freeform patterns excluded from training. Across 35,441 geometry-permittivity samples, a dilated residual network achieves average relative field errors of 1.4%-7.6%. For 6,950 inverse-designed metalens samples, the three most accurate architectures predict transmitted power with median relative errors of 0.7%-0.9%. Accuracy depends on refractive index and structural scale, with greater errors for patterns coarser than those used for training. These results demonstrate transfer to independently constructed geometries and to new spatial arrangements of dielectric values not represented in the training. Random-pattern training therefore supports reuse of electromagnetic surrogates across multiple structural families, providing a basis for sharing training costs among material screening, iterative optical design, and fabrication-tolerance analysis.

articles.title: Controlling exceptional points of layered non-Hermitian structures with magnetic field
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exceptional points are the characteristic features of non-Hermitian systems providing numerous applications in optics, acoustics, electronics, etc. We show that exceptional points can be controlled with the external magnetic field by considering the archetypal three-layered PT-symmetric photonic structure including a magneto-optic material between the loss and gain layers. Application of the magnetic field makes the system anisotropic with the polarization-sensitive reflection and transmission properties. As a result, the magnetic field can stimulate PT-symmetry breaking and mode exchange at realistic values of system parameters. Moreover, we suggest that the proposed scheme can be also used for magnetic-perturbation sensing with an easily adaptable level of desired field strength. Our results contain a valuable evidence for the usefulness of anisotropic (including magnetic) materials for tunable non-Hermitian photonics.

articles.title: A Multimodal Engineering GraphRAG Framework for Post-Wind-Event Building Assessment and Recovery Inference
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.28216v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-event building assessment requires linking observed physical damage to its consequences for safety, habitability, functionality, and recovery. Yet post-disaster evidence is often heterogeneous, incomplete, and distributed across images and reconnaissance reports, while recovery models typically require structured engineering inputs. This study develops a multimodal engineering Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GraphRAG) framework that connects post-wind-event damage evidence to physical consequences, building-condition states, recovery actions, and downtime. Image- and text-based evidence is transformed into a provenance-preserving, component-level representation distinguishing confirmed damage, explicit negative evidence, unresolved conditions, and temporary measures. Graph-aligned retrieval combines comparable building scenarios with explicit engineering relationships, while compatibility, contradiction, evidence-precedence, and abstention mechanisms constrain inference under partial observability. Recovery actions are derived from supported damage-consequence relationships, and downtime uncertainty is propagated through an action-dependency network using Monte Carlo simulation. The framework is demonstrated for tornado-affected low-rise residential buildings using reconnaissance and image-based evidence. Comparisons with BaselineRAG and Structured Baseline RAG show improved agreement for key building-condition and recovery outcomes, together with traceable engineering reasoning and preserved evidence provenance. Ablation analyses demonstrate the contributions of engineering context, evidence safeguards, and graph-path traversal. The results support transparent, recovery-oriented assessment from incomplete multimodal post-event evidence.

articles.title: Physics-constrained graph closures and working-point conditioning for a fast surrogate of linac beam dynamics
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.28250v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a graph neural network estimates a physical quantity, its frame, edge direction, aggregation and feature normalization decide which laws it can break. Wrong choices leave systematic errors the loss never registers. We build a linac beam-dynamics surrogate on this observation. Space charge, short-range wakefields and coherent synchrotron radiation enter as bounded closures on analytic kernels, on graphs whose frame and direction follow the interaction and whose symmetry makes the net space-charge self-force vanish for any weights. Verified without training, with randomized weights, the invariants break by five to eight orders of magnitude once the responsible feature is inverted. Per-working-point models constrained by the rms envelope equation are distilled into one model conditioned on 15 machine settings. On the 18.4~m L0+L1 section of the Shanghai soft x-ray free-electron laser linac, this model predicts the transverse beam envelope at 50 unseen settings to about 7%, with the centroid trajectory and emittance, in 0.38~s on a single Quadro RTX 6000 GPU. Training is instead dominated by a normalization choice, a data-derived output range for the beam size: at all 16 working points it lowers the starting error 2.2- to 8.5-fold and fixes the convergence speed. The remaining accuracy differences between hybrid and data-driven architectures vary with the working point and with the density of observation. The held-out error scales roughly as N⁻⁰.⁶ with the corpus size N. Whether the physics pays off where collective effects are strong, as in a magnetic bunch compressor, is in the next phase of our study.

articles.title: Exponential Growth of Turbulent Cross Helicity in Shear-Flow-Driven Turbulence
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.28424v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cross helicity, the velocity--magnetic-field correlation, is an ideal invariant of incompressible magnetohydrodynamics and constrains energy cascades and magnetic-field generation. Although cross helicity typically decays via visco-resistive effects, we analytically demonstrate that it grows exponentially in sheared inhomogeneous turbulence. This cross-helical shear instability is confirmed using three-dimensional numerical simulations. Growth requires a nonzero gradient of the Reynolds--Maxwell stress to produce turbulent cross helicity; this production overcomes effective losses when shear exceeds a threshold set by the ratio of turbulent magnetic to momentum diffusivities.

articles.title: Exact Nonsymmetric Vacuum Magnetic Fields with Nested Toroidal Surfaces
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.28466v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a constructive method for exact vacuum magnetic fields whose lines fill nested toroidal surfaces in ordinary space, without continuous spatial symmetry. Complex potential theory on an algebraic curve, combined with doubly periodic traveling waves from soliton theory, gives closed forms for the field, its potential and a surface label. Free parameters set the rotational transform and the magnetic shear, including exactly constant irrational transform. The same fields are exact potential flows with toroidal stream surfaces, and give stringent tests for standard stellarator codes.

articles.title: Design and Characterization of High Efficiency Single-stage Electromagnetic Coil Guns
articles.abstract: arXiv:2410.07594v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This study presents several novel approaches to improve the efficiency of a single-stage coil gun. Conventional designs typically feature a uniformly wound solenoid and a ferrite projectile. For our research, we constructed a microcontroller-based prototype to test several new enhancements, including the use of a bipolar current pulse, a stepped multilayer coil with non-uniform winding densities, and the replacement of conventional ferrite projectiles with a neodymium permanent magnet. These modifications were designed to reduce energy loss and improve projectile acceleration by changing magnetic field strength and effectively controlling the magnetic flux. The experimental results show that the proposed methods resulted in significant efficiency improvements, with the varying current pulse and stepped coil design providing enhanced magnetic force at key points in the projectile's path, and the permanent magnet projectile contributing to higher velocities and efficiencies by leveraging the current pulses. Our findings suggest that combining these enhancements significantly improves coil gun performance, achieving higher velocities and efficiencies. These findings can be applied to future coil gun developments, such as multi-stage coil gun systems.

articles.title: Searching for axions with quantum interferometry
articles.abstract: arXiv:2604.13181v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum phase measurements offer a complementary route to axion searches. We show that axion-photon interactions can imprint both Aharonov-Bohm (AB) and Berry phases in experimentally motivated quantum setups. For a coherently oscillating axion dark matter background, the induced effective current generates a time dependent magnetic flux in an rf-SQUID, leading to a measurable voltage signal through the Josephson phase. For representative benchmarks, this AB phase search reaches the minimum axion-photon coupling gₐγγmⁱⁿsim 7.8×10⁻¹⁴~GeV⁻¹ at axion mass mₐsim 10⁻¹⁰~eV, with projected sensitivity that can improve on existing limits in that parameter space by roughly one to two orders of magnitude. We also identify a geometric phase observable in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer with an adiabatically rotating magnetic field, providing a proof-of-principle phase-based probe of meV-scale axions even when they do not constitute the dark matter, although sensitivity on the coupling remains weaker than current bounds with conservative tabletop benchmarks. Extending the analysis to a three level photon-axion quasiparticle (AQP)-axion system, with the AQP realized in a topological magnetic insulator, we find a potentially measurable THz Berry phase dominated by the AQP sector, furnishing a nontrivial validation of the formalism in a richer coupled system. These setups establish quantum phase observables as a useful new framework for axion searches, with immediate phenomenological promise in superconducting circuits and longer term potential in quantum enhanced interferometry.

articles.title: Searching for ultralight bosons with Josephson junction interferometry
articles.abstract: arXiv:2604.23879v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ultralight bosons sourced by macroscopic objects can generate long-range spin-independent and spin-dependent potentials that are accessible to precision interferometry. Such potentials induce phase shifts in Josephson junctions, detectable through precision current measurements. We propose three experimental scenarios to probe photophilic scalar interactions, Lorentz-violating scalar-mediated interactions, and axion-mediated monopole-dipole interactions, depending on the nature (unpolarized or polarized) of the source. The proposed setups provide sensitivities to novel mixed couplings that are largely unconstrained by existing bounds and enables the exploration of new forces at centimeter to micrometer length scales.

articles.title: Counterexamples to the total-current Hohenberg-Kohn conjecture
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27294v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The total-current Hohenberg-Kohn conjecture asserts that the ground-state particle density and total current determine the scalar potential up to an additive constant and the vector potential up to a gauge transformation. We give three counterexamples for two spinless fermions in the physically relevant setting of three spatial dimensions. In each, a Hamiltonian Hv,A has a nondegenerate ground state with identically zero total current but nonzero magnetic field. Complex conjugation then yields a second Hamiltonian Hv,⁻A, with the same scalar potential and interaction, whose ground state has the same density and the same zero current, while the magnetic field is reversed. The first two examples are noninteracting. One is explicit, with a smooth bounded vector potential and a Gaussian density. The other has smooth bounded scalar and vector potentials in the standard potential spaces. The third example has Coulomb repulsion with unit coupling, an isotropic harmonic scalar potential, and Dirac monopole fields of magnetic charge ± 1/2. The monopole example uses vector potentials defined on separate spatial patches, since these fields are not curls of globally defined smooth vector potentials.

articles.title: Field demonstration of a self-contained 10 km mobile-to-ground quantum network node via common-aperture co-propagation
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27427v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this work, we demonstrate a dual-function, common-aperture free-space optical system that simultaneously supports decoy-state BB84 quantum key distribution (QKD) at 803 nm and bidirectional classical laser communication at 640/660 nm over a 10.31 km terrestrial link from a mobile platform to a stationary ground station. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first field demonstration of a fully integrated common-aperture architecture where a co-propagating classical optical link simultaneously performs full QKD post-processing and ecrypted payload transmission over a 10 km atmospheric channel. The classical link utilizes Manchester-coded on-off keying (MC-OOK) at 10 MHz, achieving a packet error rate of sim 0.4 % (estimated bit error rate (BER) of 3.13 × 10⁻⁵) with hardware-based self-synchronization and error-packet retransmission. Over the 10.31 km link, the QKD system achieved an average quantum bit error rate (QBER) of 2.512 % and an average secret key rate of 644 bps using rate-adaptive low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. Finally, using the distilled keys, real-time AES-256 encrypted image transmission was executed over the co-aligned classical optical channel, proving the feasibility of a completely self-contained, jam resistant mobile quantum optical network.

articles.title: Single-photon time qubit: Quantum-vacuum control and complementarity of the arrow of time
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27639v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Treating the arrow of time as a controllable quantum variable rather than a fixed external parameter is a central challenge in quantum physics. Recently, Bloch~citeBloch2025 proposed the theoretical concept of a emphtime qubit, a two-level control space H_T=spanket+,ket- that selects between opposite Hamiltonian evolutions hatH±=hatH₀±hatV, but this paradigm has remained experimentally unrealized. Here we formulate the quantum-optical theory of a single-photon time qubit---uncovering quantum-vacuum control and complementarity of the arrow of time---and experimentally probe and validate its predictions using phase-resolved single-photon interferometry from two coherently seeded entangled nonlinear biphoton sources~citeLee2018,Yoon2021. First, we show theoretically and verify experimentally that a controlled π pump--seed phase inversion during pair creation from the quantum vacuum flips the stimulated displacement generator hatV→ -hatV on top of the spontaneous two-mode squeezing background hatH₀, reversing the stimulated evolution time [hatUₛₜᵢₘ,₋(t)=hatUₛₜᵢₘ,₊(-t)] and enabling universal single-qubit SU(2) control and postselection-free first-order tomography on the temporal Bloch sphere. Second, we prove that spontaneous idler vacuum fluctuations record complete which-branch (temporal-direction) information whereas the shared coherent seed erases it without cascading or aligning the idler beams, establishing an exact wave--particle complementarity law |bmr|=V=|α|²/(1+|α|²) for the purity of the arrow of time and enabling direct first-order measurement of the Loschmidt time-reversal echo.

articles.title: Neural Operator Splitting for Fluid Dynamics in Complex Geometry
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27671v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Solving dynamical systems in complex and diverse geometries remains challenging for both numerical solvers and learning-based surrogate models. We propose Neural Operator Splitting, a framework for learning fluid dynamics while preserving the physical structure of fractional-step numerical schemes. Instead of learning the full-step evolution monolithically, we decompose each time step into physically interpretable steps, and learn each operator separately using intermediate states from the underlying numerical solver. Guided by the linearity properties of the fractional steps, we introduce a conditional-linear Fourier neural operator (CL-FNO) whose linear state mappings are modulated by nonlinear conditioning on inputs such as boundary geometry. We further introduce two complementary strategies, symmetry sampling and corrective cycling, to mitigate error accumulation during autoregressive rollout. Experiments on 2D and 3D fluid flows with varying geometries and initial conditions show that our full model reduces mean relative L² rollout error by 68% in 2D and 40% in 3D compared with a single full-step neural operator. At comparable error levels, neural-operator inference is approximately 10³ times faster per step than the Monte Carlo solver.

articles.title: Narrowband nonreciprocal transmission in a Doppler-broadened multilevel atomic system
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27792v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We theoretically investigate narrowband nonreciprocal transmission in a Doppler-broadened five-level M-type atomic medium. After Doppler averaging, the M-type system retains a narrow near-resonant electromagnetically induced transparency window that is narrower than that of a standard three-level Λ system. This spectral narrowing is associated with the decreasing separation between the two inner dressed states as atomic velocity increases. The transparency window exhibits pronounced direction-dependent transmission, with high forward transmission and strong suppression in the reverse direction. The transparency linewidth and forward-backward probe transmission can be controlled via two independent driving fields, while the central transparency frequency is kept essentially unchanged. The resulting narrowband nonreciprocity supports high forward transmission together with strong suppression in the reverse direction, which is suitable for frequency-selective optical filtering and nonreciprocal optical transmission in thermal atomic media. Our scheme with these specific features is geared towards enabling compact vapor-cell-based nonreciprocal devices for quantum network applications.

articles.title: Rapid Variability of Radiative Signatures from Driven Relativistic Reconnection
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.28034v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rapid variability in energetic flares is a distinctive feature of high-energy emission from many magnetically dominated astrophysical sources. We investigate the radiative variability of driven relativistic magnetic reconnection using Particle-in-Cell simulations of strongly magnetized flux tubes pushed to merge at driving speed vᵣₘ ₚᵤₛₕ. This setup captures the onset of reconnection and provides a controlled model for single reconnection-driven flares near compact objects, where magnetic structures can be twisted, sheared, and forced to merge by turbulent accretion flows or relativistic frame dragging. We find that the merger efficiently accelerates particles into nonthermal distributions, producing synchrotron emission whose variability tracks the reconnection phases. We identify two regimes: a quasi-steady, weakly driven regime for vₚᵤₛₕ≤0.1,c, and strongly driven regime for vᵣₘ ₚᵤₛₕ>0.1,c. The transition occurs when the driving exceeds the typical inflow-to-outflow velocity ratio of sim0.1 in steady collisionless relativistic reconnection, i.e., the average rate at which reconnection can process incoming flux, potentially providing an additional source of variability. The lightcurves rise on 1--3 light-crossing times of the reconnecting region, and the particle spectra develop power laws with index psimeq1.8--2.4. These timescales are compatible with observed variability in high-energy sources, including the very-high-energy flares of M87^* and the γ-ray flares of the Crab Nebula, making this model a viable framework for rapid flaring in active galactic nuclei and pulsar wind nebulae.

articles.title: Deriving Interplanetary Sector Boundary Crossings using Potential Field Source Surface Modeling
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.28123v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Heliospheric Current Sheet (HCS) and associated interplanetary sector boundaries fundamentally structure the solar wind environment, modulating coronal mass ejection (CME) evolution and solar energetic particle transport. In this study, we evaluate the capability of a static Potential Field Source Surface (PFSS; Rₛₛ=2.5R_odot) coronal model to directly map interplanetary sector boundary crossings from the Sun to 1 au without dynamic heliospheric propagation models. We compare ballistically transported HCS crossings derived from GONG-ADAPT and SDO/HMI magnetic maps against sector boundary crossing observations from the SBCross catalog. PFSS modeling reproduces the large-scale interplanetary magnetic field topology well (Japprox0.50), achieving hit rates (POD) of 0.64 for GONG-ADAPT and 0.76 for HMI. Carrington synoptic maps outperform flux-transport modeled maps, suggesting that the short-term observational noise from data assimilation degrades topological matching more than map "aging". Predictive skill shows a strong solar cycle dependence, performing significantly better during solar maxima (POD=0.70-0.81) than solar minima (POD=0.56-0.67), attributed to more distinct crossings due to higher HCS inclination angles during maximum. Matched events exhibit travel times close to ballistic estimates of 4.8-4.9 days with an average timing difference centered near zero (±1.1 days) and 90% of events within ± 1.8 days. The hit rate of HCS structures that interact with CMEs does not degrade (POD = 0.67-0.83), despite propagating approx7 hours faster on average, implying that the CME interaction causes only minor structural changes to the HCS. Larger timing differences (>24 hours) are associated with flatter current sheets. Overall, static PFSS extrapolations offer a computationally inexpensive, effective approach for mapping global sector boundary structure.

articles.title: Detection and Statistics of large-scale Sector Boundary Crossings in the Solar Wind: The SBCross Catalog
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.28139v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Heliospheric sector boundary crossings (SBCs), composed of the Heliospheric Current Sheet (HCS), Heliospheric Plasma Sheet (HPS), and surrounding plasma halo, represent fundamental structures in the solar wind that influence interplanetary dynamics and space weather. We present the textscSBCross catalog, an automated, publicly available database containing 1,076 SBC events derived from in-situ observations spanning more than 30 years (1995--2026), covering Solar Cycles 23 and 24 alongside the rising and maximum phases of Solar Cycle 25. By combining interplanetary magnetic field (IMF) and 255~eV suprathermal electron pitch angle distributions (PAD) data, our algorithm reliably captures large-scale polarity transitions, with 76% of detected SBCs exhibiting clear HPS signatures (β > 1, nₚₑₐₖ > 10mathrm,cm⁻³). Across the catalog, we find an average occurrence rate of approx 2.6 events per Carrington rotation, a median event duration of approx 9.0,hours, and a median physical thickness of approx 7.4 × 10⁶,km. Furthermore, approximately approx 15% of detected SBCs interact with interplanetary coronal mass ejections (CMEs) on average, with this proportion rising up to 33% during solar maximum. These CME-associated events exhibit systematically longer durations (median of 10.0,hours), 54% larger physical thicknesses, and higher average solar wind velocities. Notably, all high-velocity SBC events (> 600mathrm,km,s⁻¹) are exclusively driven by CME interactions, demonstrating local plasma pile-up and structural entanglement resulting from fast CMEs overtaking the ambient slow background. The textscSBCross catalog serves as an updated successor to the classic SBC list by L. Svalgaard, delivering a standardized, open-access resource for the heliophysics community to systematically investigate sector boundary transitions.

articles.title: A Solar Optical Clock
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.28485v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Precision spectroscopy underpins quantum sensing, atomic timekeeping, and the search for terrestrial-mass exoplanets. Finding an Earth-Sun analog requires fractional splitting of spectral features that rivals the precision of the best laboratory spectroscopy. This corresponds to resolution of a few parts in 10⁵ of a typical stellar spectral line, or a Doppler velocity precision of less than 10 cm s⁻¹. Only a few astrophysical spectrometers reach this regime, and only by dispersing starlight with large gratings and averaging thousands of lines. Here, we show that comparable precision can be achieved on a single solar line by leveraging techniques used in quantum sensors and optical clocks. A laser is frequency-locked to the 1565 nm solar Fe I line by coupling to a single mode of the solar thermal field and counted against an optical frequency comb referenced to the SI second, thus creating a solar optical clock. Operating at the fundamental photon-noise limit of thermal heterodyne spectroscopy, we achieve centroid precision of one part in 10⁹ of the optical frequency, or 30 cm s⁻¹ in radial velocity. We recover the Sun's five-minute acoustic oscillations and the expected Rossiter-McLaughlin signal during a solar eclipse. Combining these techniques from quantum sensing with a thirty-meter-class telescope could enable our demonstrated precision on the nearest Sun-like stars in a few hours. Multiplexing such absolute frequency measurements across lines with different magnetic sensitivity and formation depth would reduce averaging time and help disentangle stellar granulation and activity from the Doppler signature of terrestrial exoplanets, providing new approaches to address some of the most demanding measurements in astrophysical spectroscopy.

articles.title: Automated optimization of solar energetic particle acceleration and transport parameters against five-spacecraft observations of the 9 October 2021 event
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.28603v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Solar energetic particle (SEP) events threaten space infrastructure, yet physics-based prediction models depend on numerous poorly constrained free parameters. We introduce the Fujitsu Solar Energetic particle Intelligent Tuning and Evaluation Network (SEITEN), which couples the SUSANOO MHD model of CME propagation to SEPIF, a diffusive shock acceleration and focused transport model, through the shock conditions SUSANOO supplies, and automatically optimizes the free parameters of the particle model against the SEP event of 9 October 2021. The mean free path and the injection efficiency vary independently along each magnetic field line and heliolongitudinal bin, giving a 19-dimensional problem solved by quasi-Monte Carlo sampling followed by a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator. The optimized model reproduces proton flux profiles at five spacecraft with a mean absolute error of approx 0.45 in log₁₀ flux, and the inferred mean free paths show a clear east-west structure; these are effective parameters conditional on the assumed transport geometry. Six independent runs show that whether mean free paths or injection efficiencies dominate depends on the MHD shock strength, and that injection efficiencies differ by orders of magnitude between MHD configurations despite nearly identical fit quality. Joint MHD-SEP parameter estimation is therefore a necessary next step towards generalized, operational SEP forecasting.

articles.title: The Impact of Mahjong on Marital Relationships
articles.abstract: arXiv:2404.16871v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: One of the national treasures, Mahjong, is a strategic card game originating from China, played competitively by constructing and optimizing card hands among four players. In the game, players aim to achieve specific combinations of cards, known as "winning hands," through actions such as drawing, discarding, pung, and kong. Mahjong not only tests memory and strategy but also integrates probability and chance, embodying profound cultural significance and social attributes. However, as Mahjong becomes a widely popular social activity, its impact on personal life has gradually become apparent. In this paper, I delve into the analysis of the effects of playing Mahjong on marital relationships, particularly the three negative effects it brings to women: Time Displacement: The uncertainty of Mahjong playing time leads to a reduction in shared time between spouses. Women may feel neglected due to the lack of companionship, leading to "Mahjong Panic Syndrome." Emotional Conflict: Mahjong playing can result in losses, and men may harbor "resentment from defeat" at the Mahjong table, which could be brought into the household and spark marital disputes. Social Isolation: Women may feel excluded from their partner's social circle if they do not participate in Mahjong activities, experiencing "marginalization at the card table." This study not only reveals the potential negative impact of late-night Mahjong returns on marital relationships but also provides new insights into communication and empathy between spouses from the perspectives of decision trees, time series analysis, and game theory. It also finds the optimal solution through Monte Carlo simulations.

articles.title: Physics-informed sampler for solver-free data generation in operator learning
articles.abstract: arXiv:2509.00867v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neural operators offer fast surrogates for parametric PDEs but typically rely on costly datasets generated by repeated numerical solves. We propose a physics-informed sampler (PI-sampler) that generates PDE-consistent input--solution pairs without numerical PDE solves. The sampler draws candidate solution fields from neural-network priors and uses automatic differentiation to evaluate the governing differential, boundary, and initial-condition operators, yielding consistent training tuples by construction. Unlike solution-first methods based on analytical bases or precomputed solutions, it requires neither problem-specific basis functions nor seed simulations. The resulting PDE inputs follow an implicit pushforward distribution, which can be characterized for linear operators in the Gaussian-process limit of Bayesian neural networks but is generally non-Gaussian for nonlinear operators. We integrate the PI-sampler with a function encoder and Transformer-based neural operator and test it on reaction--diffusion equations, Poisson equations on parameterized geometries, time-dependent Sine--Gordon dynamics, a five-dimensional PDE, and flexible-cylinder vortex-induced vibration. The models generalize to independently prescribed forcing distributions, zero forcing, mixed boundary conditions, and unseen geometries. Experiments with DeepONet confirm that the generated data also support other operator architectures. In problem-specific benchmarks, sampling is approximately 51 times faster on CPU and 850 times faster on GPU than numerical solvers. The PI-sampler thus provides an efficient approach to data generation and augmentation that complements high-fidelity simulation.

articles.title: Edge turbulence controlled by topologically self-optimized fluxes in fusion devices
articles.abstract: arXiv:2603.28633v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The magnetic field topology undergoes a drastic transition near the separatrix in magnetic confinement fusion devices, inducing topological chaos. This phenomenon is investigated across tokamaks, stellarators, and the RFX-mod reversed-field pinch. Within this boundary region, self-optimized fluxes of shear-generated magnetic and cross-helicity, together with the ensemble-averaged magnetic moment, are hypothesized to govern plasma stability, self-organization, and transport. By treating the averaged magnetic moment as an active scalar and using the Fokker-Planck equation to reconcile kinetic and fluid descriptions, this study couples its dynamics with a novel multichannel, self-optimized helicity cascade loop. The derived spectral laws for the floating potential and ion saturation current agree with measurements from numerous experiments. Distributed chaos theory quantifies the randomness of the observed states, revealing that a narrow layer at the separatrix suppresses strong core randomness, transforming it into distributed chaos in the scrape-off layer. A constrained variational principle for active control has also been considered. Tuning Lagrangian multipliers via helicity injection drives the system toward an attractor state that stabilizes the separatrix shear layer, suppresses edge-localized modes, and spreads the heat load, using magnetic reconnection as a nonlinear solver. This framework circumvents conventional diffusive limitations, providing an analytical foundation to model heat-load patterns and stochastic ripple loss in next-step devices.

articles.title: Widely tunable SNAP microresonators induced at the optical fiber intersections
articles.abstract: arXiv:2604.06960v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A widely tunable free spectral range (FSR) is essential for many microresonator applications, but achieving it in compact high-Q systems remains a significant challenge. Surface nanoscale axial photonics (SNAP) provides a route to such devices by localizing whispering-gallery modes through nanoscale effective-radius variations along an optical fiber. Recently, it has been experimentally demonstrated that side-coupling between two optical fibers can induce high-Q SNAP microresonators. In contrast to broadly explored monolithic microresonators, this configuration enables extensive mechanical tuning of the microresonator configuration and FSR through fiber bending, tilting, and twisting. Here, we develop the theory of SNAP microresonators induced at optical fiber intersections, which has remained largely unexplored. We consider weakly twisted fibers, whose geometry can be decomposed into tilting and bending. We show that extremely small fiber curvature critically affects the coupling-induced cutoff frequency variation, the shape of the effective axial potential, and the spectrum of the induced resonator. We discuss the physical origin of this curvature and show that accounting for it resolves the discrepancy between theory and experiment. These findings establish side-coupled optical fibers as a simple, reconfigurable platform for realizing microresonators with a widely tunable FSR.

articles.title: Performance of the TUCAN Magnetically Shielded Room
articles.abstract: arXiv:2604.15565v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The TRIUMF Ultracold Advanced Neutron (TUCAN) collaboration has commissioned a large magnetically shielded room to be used for measuring the neutron electric dipole moment (nEDM) to a precision of 10⁻²⁷~ecm. The room is composed of five layers of MuMetal and one layer of copper and sits within the lesssim 370~muT ambient field produced by the TRIUMF cyclotron. Within this environment, the quasi-static shielding factor was measured to be 2.95(2) × 10⁴ at 0.01~Hz with an external peak-to-peak perturbation of 2~muT. Without the large ambient cyclotron field, the shielding factor improves to 3.40(3)× 10⁴ at the same perturbation amplitude and frequency. After idealization in the cyclotron field, the residual field at the room center was B = 1.8(2)~nT and the vertical first-order gradient across the central 1~m³ (dBz/dz) was -307(26)~pT/m. With additional improvement to the idealization, and with active compensation, we expect the room to be adequate for a 10⁻²⁷~ecm nEDM search.

articles.title: Excited-state Properties Beyond the Excitation Energy from Orbital-Optimized Density Functional Calculations I: Dipole Moments of Rydberg States
articles.abstract: arXiv:2606.12272v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rydberg excited states are challenging to describe due to their highly diffuse character. Orbital-optimized density functional calculations typically provide more accurate values of the excitation energy of Rydberg states than time-dependent density functional theory approaches, but their performance with respect to excited-state properties such as the dipole moment remains largely unexplored as existing benchmarks are limited to the lowest excited state. Here, orbital-optimized density functional calculations with a plane-wave basis set are used to compute the dipole moment of several Rydberg states of a set of small molecules. Plane waves provide a flexible representation of diffuse Rydberg orbitals, whereas commonly used atomic orbitals basis sets are found to yield significant discrepancies in the magnitude and orientation of the dipole moment, even when diffuse functions are included and the excitation energy agrees well with the plane-wave results. The generalized gradient approximation functional PBE used in combination with the plane-wave representation of the orbitals gives good agreement with higher-level coupled-cluster calculations performed with sufficiently diffuse basis sets, when the latter are available. The hybrid functional PBE0 further improves the results, while PBE with globally scaled explicit Perdew-Zunger self-interaction correction generally leads to larger errors and an overestimation of the dipole moment, despite restoring the correct asymptotic -1/r dependence of the effective Kohn--Sham potential.

articles.title: Resonant lunar tides of Earth's core and basal magma ocean
articles.abstract: arXiv:2606.16340v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Earth's magnetic field is generated by fluid motion in the liquid-metal core and has been active for billions of years. However, prior to the onset of inner-core growth, the sources of mechanical power that drove the geodynamo remain uncertain. During this period, the core may have been overlain by a basal magma ocean (BMO), creating two immiscible fluid layers separated by a density interface, beneath the solid mantle. We develop a theory for lunar tides in this core--BMO system, in which the tidal potential acts on the density contrast between the two layers. The resulting dynamics differ fundamentally from previous models driven by imposed deformation of the core's bounding envelope. In the inviscid limit, the response transitions from an equilibrium tide to an interfacial gravity wave as forcing frequency increases. The two regimes are separated by a resonance that occurs when the forcing frequency matches the natural frequency of the degree-2, order-2 interfacial mode. The inviscid core flow is formally identical to the canonical elliptical vortex, linking the problem to the theory of elliptical instability. Finite viscosity regularises the resonance, introduces phase lag and generates oscillatory boundary layers. Combined with parameterised models of lunar recession and BMO crystallisation, the theory predicts enhanced core-boundary ellipticity, core-flow speed, magnetic Reynolds number and instability metrics, particularly near resonance. These results identify a previously unexplored mechanism for tidally driven flow in differentiated planetary bodies and show that a BMO can enhance tidal coupling to the core, potentially contributing to dynamo action.

articles.title: Semi-local Floquet theory for active azimuthal magnetic modulation of Hall-thruster high-frequency instabilities
articles.abstract: arXiv:2606.21265v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a semi-local Floquet model to screen active azimuthal magnetic modulation as a control approach for high-frequency drift instabilities in Hall thrusters. The uniform-field kinetic response supplies a local kernel for a finite sideband matrix, and stability is measured by the upper growth envelope over the Bloch zone. Root searches include both frequency branches, continuation, singular-value validation, and contour root counts. At the reference normalized parallel wave number k_z = 0.045, for sinusoidal profiles with periods of 10, 20, and 40 mm, every nonzero sampled modulation amplitude increases both the peak and integrated positive Bloch-zone growth. The uniform-field reference is already unstable, so these increases describe faster linear amplification rather than the onset of instability from a stable state. At a period of 20 mm and relative amplitude 0.5, the peak and integral increase by 26.74 and 26.44 percent, respectively; this large amplitude requires caution within the semi-local ordering. Selected projected wave-number windows still show reductions, but these coexist with enhanced global growth and do not establish stabilization. A supplementary parallel-wave-number scan finds weak global growth reduction at k_z = 0.09: at 20 mm and amplitude 0.3, the peak and integral decrease by 0.300 and 0.299 percent, respectively, while the spectrum remains unstable. The sign and magnitude of the modulation effect therefore depend on the tested plasma parameters; neither these small reductions nor the local projected changes establish improved nonlinear transport.

articles.title: Exact 1D Nonlinear Solutions for Proton-Driven Plasma Wakefields
articles.abstract: arXiv:2607.06458v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We extend the classical 1D nonlinear relativistic plasma wakefield paradigm to evaluate the pristine fluid profiles driven by intense relativistic proton trains under the comoving coordinate approximation. Using an intense two-bunch scheme, our adaptive integration model is validated down to machine precision against exact closed-form cold-fluid invariants, confirming that interface boundary corners represent physical step discontinuities in the second potential derivative. Scaling to an N=100 micro-bunch train, we resolve macroscopic phase-accumulation and subsequent nonlinear detuning by deriving a closed-form, parameter-free piecewise analytical envelope expression. This solution successfully maps the initial unattenuated quadratic coherent growth alongside the flat asymptotic horizontal saturation horizon governed by nonlinear energy conservation. Furthermore, the framework analytically evaluates the transient envelope overshoot, tracking its decay onto the saturation boundary via an exact phase-slip integration length scale. Providing immediate, ready macro-envelope bounds, this computationally inexpensive tool eliminates empirical adjustments and yields a robust mathematical baseline designed to guide and accelerate complex, multi-dimensional particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations through rapid parameter space exploration before deploying heavy computational assets. It establishes an efficient foundation to optimize asymmetric, custom-shaped driver profiles required to break the fundamental symmetric transformer ratio limit of 2 to make current particle accelerators more efficient.

articles.title: Repurposing acquisition devices into trigger-based timing synchronization of breakdown events during MITICA high voltage holding experiments
articles.abstract: arXiv:2607.08501v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A critical requirement for MITICA -- a full-scale prototype of the heating Neutral Beam Injectors hosted at the Consorzio RFX Neutral Beam Test Facility for the ITER experiment -- is the capability to withstand a continuous voltage of 1MV across the vacuum gaps insulating the beam source from the grounded vessel. To validate such feature, a dedicated voltage-holding test campaign was conducted throughout 2024 and 2025 using a full-scale mock-up of the beam source. The tests also involved an accurate characterization of the associated breakdown events: vacuum dielectric failures which result in rapid potential drops and generate strong current discharges. This contribution will present a relative time reconstruction architecture based on cost-effective, embedded RedPitaya (Zynq-7000 FPGA) devices repurposed as timing hubs. These nodes function as configurable trigger multiplexers while simultaneously recording trigger signals as transients to facilitate the offline reconstruction of event sequences. The method allows self-calibration through measuring the static intrinsic delays of the optical fibers and internal logics, generating delay offsets to synchronize acquired waveforms across a sparse, connected-graph topology of both acquisition devices and hubs themselves.

articles.title: Decoding Transient X-ray Absorption Spectra of Acetylacetone With Multireference Algebraic Diagrammatic Construction Theory
articles.abstract: arXiv:2608.09747v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Time-resolved X-ray absorption spectroscopy (TR-XAS) offers an element- and site-specific probe of coupled electronic and nuclear dynamics, but its interpretation requires methods that can treat multiconfigurational excited states across nonequilibrium nuclear ensembles. Here, we report time-resolved simulations of the acetylacetone (AcAc) transient X-ray absorption spectra by combining surface-hopping dynamics from complete active space second-order perturbation theory with multireference algebraic diagrammatic construction (MR-ADC). The simulated 20-200 fs spectra show a good agreement with experimental measurements and reveal that the TR-XAS response is governed by continuously evolving distributions of molecular geometries on the singlet potential energy surfaces (S2 and S1). In particular, absorption at 279.5-281.5 eV is enhanced for transient, nearly symmetric proton-sharing configurations, whereas the 284-286 eV profile reflects geometry-dependent C1s excitations modulated by proton transfer, bond alternation, and ring opening. For the long-time T₁ spectrum (7-10 ps), the principal features near 281.4 and 283.8 eV are assigned to central C 1s excitations into low-lying triplet pi-orbitals. Together, our simulations provide a more complete mechanistic picture of AcAc photorelaxation by directly linking ultrafast carbon K-edge signals to proton transfer, skeletal reorganization, internal conversion, and triplet formation.

articles.title: Ising-machine-like Driving Condition Restrictions in SSBM and Additional Pseudo-annealing- Driving Method for SSBM that Achieves Best Cut Value Search -
articles.abstract: arXiv:2608.12545v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In our previous work, we proposed and experimentally demonstrated a physics-based simulator for combinatorial optimization problems (SSBM), which exploits a distinctive spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB) phenomenon identified in a dissipative system exhibiting robust causality described by an iterative equation. We further conducted numerical simulations in which initial fluctuations of distinct patterns were applied to large-scale benchmark problems, and reported that the SSBM exhibits a unique behavior absent in conventional Ising machines: under specific conditions, pseudo-spin patterns progressively converge during the solution-search process and ultimately coalesce into a single pattern, with the cut value of the converged solution reaching 99.7% of the best-known cut value. In the present paper, we elucidate the conditions under which the SSBM can be configured to emulate the behavior of a continuous-variable Ising machine. We further demonstrate that by additionally incorporating an effect analogous to physical annealing into these conditions, the SSBM becomes capable of identifying the best-known cut value for the K₂₀₀₀ benchmark instance.

articles.title: Low-rank approximation of Moment Tensor Potential enables reducing training set size without loss of accuracy
articles.abstract: arXiv:2609.07372v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this study, we implement a low-rank approximation of Moment Tensor Potential (MTP) based on the tensor train (TT) decomposition. The implemented tensor-factorized MTP (TFMTP) and the original MTP model are actively trained via a MaxVol-based algorithm during molecular dynamics simulations of a four-component molten salt mixture, LiF-NaF-KF (FLiNaK), and geometry optimizations of a five-component equiatomic Mo-Nb-Ta-W-V random alloy. We demonstrate that under a 1.5-fold compression, TFMTP requires two times fewer configurations for fitting than the original MTP model, while maintaining an indistinguishable level of accuracy. These actively trained MTP and TFMTP models are further used to evaluate the density and viscosity of FLiNaK at temperatures ranging from 600 to 1200 K, as well as the elastic constants and bulk modulus of the Mo-Nb-Ta-W-V alloy at zero temperature. For both atomic systems, the differences in physical properties predicted by MTP and TFMTP are negligible.

articles.title: Inference of Hierarchical Core-Periphery Structure in Temporal Networks
articles.abstract: arXiv:2506.10135v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Networks can have various types of mesoscale structures. One such structure is core--periphery structure, which consists of sets of densely-connected core nodes and sets of sparsely-connected peripheral nodes. Core nodes are connected densely to other core nodes and are potentially connected densely to peripheral nodes, which are connected sparsely to other nodes. There has been much research on core--periphery structure in time-independent networks, but few core--periphery detection methods have been developed for time-dependent (i.e., ``temporal") networks. Using a multilayer-network representation of temporal networks and an inference approach that employs stochastic block models, we generalize a recent method for detecting hierarchical core--periphery structure citePolanco23 from time-independent networks to temporal networks. In contrast to ``onion-like'' nested core--periphery structures (where each node is assigned to a group according to how deeply it is nested in a network's core), hierarchical core--periphery structures encompass networks with nested structures, tree-like structures (where any two groups must either be disjoint or have one group as a strict subset of the other group), and general non-nested mesoscale structures (where the group assignments of nodes do not have to be nested in any way). To perform statistical inference and thereby identify hierarchical core--periphery structure, we use a Markov-chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) approach. We illustrate our method for detecting hierarchical core--periphery structure in one synthetic temporal network and two real-world temporal networks, and we discuss the structures that we identify in these networks.

articles.title: Operator learning for efficient quantum computation
articles.abstract: arXiv:2606.20184v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: An efficient implementation of quantum algorithms is often hindered by the lack of efficient primitives for operators and state preparation. This limits both the ability of near-term quantum hardware to simulate complex problems and the potential of fault-tolerant algorithms to achieve practical quantum advantage. To address this, we propose a framework that maps discrete operators onto compact, structured quantum circuits. The resulting variational circuits can be tailored to the connectivity and long-range interaction of the target hardware. The learning process employs backpropagation together with a cost function that efficiently optimizes unitary operators and non-unitary --dense or sparse-- operators using only a single ancilla qubit for block encoding. Additionally, we introduce a regularization term that reduces the approximation error. The approach is validated for both quantum mechanical and engineering applications. In the former case, we learn propagators that arise in native quantum problems --such as quantum simulation and quantum chemistry-- and achieve improved resource scaling in comparison to standard Suzuki--Trotter expansions. In the latter case, we demonstrate the approach's ability to implement the second-order central finite difference approximation of the Laplace operator --relevant for solving partial differential equations-- while improving upon current error metrics. The final example deals with learning a dense, non-unitary operator that arises in the analysis of inviscid potential flow around an airfoil. These results motivate the extension of the framework to a broader class of operator-synthesis problems beyond the prototypical engineering and quantum applications considered here.

articles.title: Cooperative control of dissipative qubits: steering along the fastest dissipative contraction
articles.abstract: arXiv:2606.30073v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In the control of dissipative quantum systems, the slow relaxation modes usually set the ultimate manipulation timescale. We show that this bottleneck can be bypassed when dissipation itself is used as the engine of the transfer. For a qubit with non-unital, anisotropic Bloch relaxation characterized by the ratio κ=T₁/T₂>1, coherent control can only rotate the Bloch vector, whereas the bath alone can change its length. The fastest transfer between two thermal states therefore consists in steering the Bloch vector, at every instant, along the direction in which the bath contracts it most rapidly. This direction is obtained in closed form and lies slightly beyond the equatorial plane. With strong pulses, the resulting minimum transfer time is a fraction of T₂, instead of several T₁ for passive relaxation. With bounded fields, the Pontryagin maximum principle yields a bang--singular--bang synthesis whose singular arc is precisely this fastest-contraction direction, and the minimum time exceeds its strong-pulse limit by a correction inversely proportional to the field amplitude. We also determine the full time--energy Pareto front: moderate accelerations require little energy, and the time optimum lies at its steep, high-energy end. Off-axis targets are treated within the same framework; their only additional benefit is a shorter final rotation. These results apply directly to magnetic-resonance spins, nitrogen-vacancy centers and superconducting qubits, all of which operate deep in the strong-pulse regime.

articles.title: Quadratic Sample Complexity for Strictly Replicable Realizable Learning with Unknown Marginals
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under the quantifier exists A,forall D, where the realizable distribution and its marginal are unknown, we determine the finite-class sample-complexity exponent for strict replicability: two independent samples and one shared seed must produce identical functions. For ε=δ=ρ=10⁻⁴, the worst case over |H|le M is Θ((log M)²), without iterated logarithms. For dge1, 0<εle1/16, and 0<δ,ρle10⁻³, every randomized, possibly improper learner valid throughout an explicit anchored realizable family requires Ω(d²/(ερ²)) samples. For the full Boolean class P_d, dge2, in the same parameter range, we prove the matching characterization Θ(d²/(ερ²)+ε⁻¹log(1/δ)) using a proper Poissonized ball-sampling algorithm. We also give an explicit proper Gibbs upper bound for every finite measurable Boolean class. Our lower bound uses square-root probabilities and volumetric packing; the Gibbs proof builds on established coupling and generalization identities. Finally, we characterize the known-marginal worst case for P_d, showing why that interface must be kept distinct.

articles.title: Learned Control Variates for Rare Grid-Outage Estimation at Electric Vehicle Charging Stations
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27159v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Public charging of electric vehicles (EVs) adds a large and synchronized load to the distribution feeders. In most networks, it is rare to overload a feeder at the same time. When it does happen, the consequences can be severe: an overloaded feeder stresses its transformers and can trigger cascading outages across a city. Planners who design for high reliability therefore need to estimate very small outage probabilities. To that end, plain Monte Carlo estimation with an expensive grid simulator can require a prohibitively large number of runs for this task. To reduce the number of runs, we propose a control variate (CV) built from a learned classifier of the outage, trained on cheap observable features such as temperature and load forecasts. We show that for any binary learner, the variance reduction is an explicit function of its recall and false-positive rate. Furthermore, we show that control variate based on a Gaussian proxy of the load loses its effect as outages become rarer, while a learner with non-vanishing precision keeps removing a fixed fraction of the variance even in the extreme rare-event regime. We verify these results in numerical experiments using a feeder-overload simulator across three orders of magnitude of outage probability and obtain that even weak learner with a single feature can remove a quarter of the variance, while a boosted-tree learner is able to remove about 60%. We then apply the estimator to the feeder network of Surabaya, Indonesia, in which the Gaussian load model leaves every feeder three to seven times the one-day-in-ten-years blackout target. At the same simulation budget, planning the reserve with the learned CV and a 95% confidence limit reduces the city-wide blackout days by a third compared with Monte Carlo. These results show that learned control variates can help planners design distribution grids that stay reliable against rare outages.

articles.title: Active Pilot Sampling for Multi-fidelity Estimation in Stochastic Optimization
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27563v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Stochastic optimization with high-fidelity nonlinear models is often computationally prohibitive because each objective evaluation requires sampling-based uncertainty quantification inside an outer optimization loop. Multi-fidelity estimators, such as approximate control variates (ACV), can reduce this cost by exploiting cheaper low-fidelity models, but they require model-output covariance information to determine control-variate weights and sample allocations. These covariances are generally unknown and must be estimated through pilot sampling. Existing pilot-sampling strategies primarily address one-off estimation and do not exploit the structure of iterative stochastic optimization, where covariance information may vary smoothly across the design domain and can be shared across optimization queries. We propose an active pilot-sampling framework that learns a probabilistic emulator of the model-output covariance matrix using a positive-definite parameterization based on matrix-logarithm-transformed correlations and log standard deviations. The emulator provides design-specific covariance estimates for constructing ACV estimators at new optimization queries, avoiding repeated independent covariance estimation at every design. Active-learning acquisition functions allocate pilot samples to designs where covariance information is most uncertain and most relevant to the outer optimization objective. We demonstrate the method on a four-branch benchmark and a multi-fidelity Bayesian optimal experimental design application for sensor placement and measurement-time selection in a convection-diffusion system. The results show improved optimization performance relative to single-fidelity Monte Carlo and simpler pilot-sampling strategies.

articles.title: From POMDP Theory to Deep RL with Particle Filters
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27575v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning in partially observable environments requires inferring hidden states, learning latent dynamics, and planning under the resulting belief. Practical algorithms often solve one aspect of the above pipeline while relying on approximations for the others that are often poorly understood, while existing POMDP theory typically analyzes computationally inefficient theoretical algorithms far from modern deep RL practice. To fill this gap, we propose a practical end-to-end algorithm that approximately solves the hidden state filtering problem via sequential Monte Carlo (SMC), updates a latent dynamics model online, and performs approximate online planning for d steps before bootstrapping leaves with a state-value critic (a QMDP approximation). We analyze each approximation and prove an end-to-end regret bound decomposing the error into model estimation error, particle filter error, Monte Carlo rollout error, and a structural bias term induced by the QMDP approximation controllable by the planning depth that we further analyze in various special cases. The resulting guarantee makes explicit how statistical sample size, particle budget, rollout budget, and planning depth affect performance. We instantiate our algorithm in an MPC-based deep RL framework, demonstrating its practicality on a variety of environments. On a POMDP that satisfies our assumptions, each term of the bound decays at its predicted rate. Our results provide a practical and theoretically grounded route for bridging theory and practice within online decision-making in POMDPs.

articles.title: Stabilizing Filters for Graph Signal Generation
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.28318v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generating graph signals is an important task in machine learning, and incorporating the underlying graph into a generative model enables structurally-informed distribution modeling. However, said graph is often noisy or imperfectly estimated, and structural errors can affect the generative process and the resulting signal distribution. While recent work has established stability guarantees for graph neural ordinary differential equations, the robustness of graph-aware reference dynamics, as used in topological Schrödinger bridge models, remains largely unexplored.
