articles.title: LatBridge: Efficient and Stable Model Replacement in Latent-Communication Multi-Agent Systems
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent systems rely on communication to complete tasks, and latent communication passes continuous representations to reduce text generation and re-encoding. However, multi-agent systems must reconfigure agent models, whereas existing latent-communication methods are built for fixed model combinations, so their interfaces may fail after replacement. Our pilot study confirms this interface failure and identifies the requirement for interface reuse after model replacement. We present LatBridge, which connects agent models through a shared Bridge and separate interfaces under a shared latent-communication protocol. After agent model replacement, LatBridge reuses unchanged interfaces, selects matching low-rank interfaces, and combines them through the Bridge, training only missing ones with all models frozen. The Bridge processes source representations in the basic mode and constructs target input without autoregressive generation in the accelerated mode. Experiments support effective communication after model replacement, with mean basic-mode accuracies of 14.8% on MATH and 27.3% on ALFWorld next-action prediction across eight small-model configurations. Analyses examine the factors supporting task accuracy and communication efficiency.

articles.title: Slot-JEPA: Object-Structured Prediction Interfaces for Latent World Models
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.28074v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As a prototypical latent world model, Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) provide strong semantic representations. However, dense patch representations expose a redundant interface to downstream predictors, which must implicitly infer spatial organization and temporal correspondence, presenting three challenges. First, object information is distributed across patches, forcing each downstream predictor to redundantly recover object structure that could otherwise be reused across tasks before modeling interactions. Second, the lack of explicit entity correspondence across time makes historical transitions expensive, restricting the predictor's flexibility in utilizing context. Third, without explicit transport structure, existing JEPA models typically use pointwise l1/l2 distances, which are insensitive to spatial displacement when predicted and goal supports are largely disjoint. We propose the Slot-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Slot-JEPA), which decomposes dense representations into stable semantic slots and time-varying spatial masks. Pretrained once and frozen downstream, this decomposition exposes a reusable object-structured interface. Building on it, our Transition Memory Predictor (TMP) stores visual transitions as compact masks and retrieves useful context using statistics of corresponding slots. Its two branches separate slot-specific dynamics from shared cross-slot dynamics. We further use Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) to supervise mask prediction and evaluate candidate plans by transporting mass between aligned predicted and goal masks, providing a signal better aligned with spatial progress. Across seven visual-understanding benchmarks, the slot-reconstructed features remain transferable. Slot-JEPA also improves goal-conditioned planning across six planar environments and four robotic arm planning tasks on the REALM-JEPA benchmark.

articles.title: A Semi-Analytical Inference Framework for Structural Causal Models
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.28103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Structural Causal Models (SCMs) provide a principled framework for observational, interventional, and counterfactual reasoning, all of which rely on probabilistic inference. Existing frameworks either transform SCMs into alternative tractable representations or rely on approximate inference with expressive generative models. We instead perform inference using a message passing scheme directly on the SCM by representing structural mechanisms and probability densities in a common finite-dimensional function space. Forward propagation combines a numerical realization of the Law of the Unconscious Statistician, while propagated densities are recovered by spline projection from LOTUS moments. The same representation naturally yields backward message passing for conditioning, providing a unified framework for causal inference. Using tensor-product B-spline bases, the resulting algorithm expresses inference through numerical quadrature and linear algebra without explicitly constructing conditional distributions. Experiments on randomly generated continuous SCMs demonstrate accurate approximation of Monte Carlo reference solutions and systematic improvement with increasing basis resolution.

articles.title: S-Agent 2.0: Spatial Reasoning with a General Coding Agent
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.28354v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatial reasoning asks a model to work out where objects are in 3D space, how they relate to one another, and how they move. Agentic VLMs have recently brought large improvements on such tasks by letting the model actively gather evidence with 3D perception tools instead of answering in a single pass. Even so, on many questions the tools return the right evidence and the model still does not arrive at the correct answer: the gap between model and tools, where raw readings become usable conclusions, is left unfilled. We present S-Agent 2.0, a spatial reasoning agent that equips an off-the-shelf general coding agent with a command-line perception toolkit, and we design the interface around one principle: help the VLM close the evidence loop: acquire scene evidence, remember it in a persistent scene memory, and interpret each reading in plain spatial language. This design keeps the full flexibility of a coding agent, and every reading it acts on stays grounded in the tools' geometry. On MMSI-Bench and ReVSI, the toolkit improves a strong open-source model, Qwen3.8-27B, by +13.9 and +20.5 points over the same agent without tools, and a strong closed-source model, Gemini-3.8-Flash, by +11.2 and +9.6 points. With the open backbone S-Agent 2.0 reaches 66.5 on MMSI-Bench and 82.3 on ReVSI, ahead of the specialized system SpatialClaw on the same backbone (62.6 and 74.5), and with Gemini-3.8-Flash it reaches 74.1 and 90.5 against its 67.0 and 79.7. Both tool gains shrink as the backbone grows more capable, but SpatialClaw's shrinks far more on ReVSI, from +13.2 to +2.7, while ours stays at +9.6. S-Agent 2.0 also works across different general coding agent harnesses, such as Codex and Claude Code.

articles.title: Evolving Agent Interfaces
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.28601v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computer-use agents are limited by the interfaces humans give them. An agent may type a spreadsheet cell by cell when a single line of code would do, or print all two thousand lines of a file through a shell to find one function. Both the interfaces and the knowledge of when to use each are built by hand, which cannot keep pace with new applications, workflows, and models. We argue that interface design should itself be an agent capability. We introduce Agent S4, an autonomous computer-use scientist that builds Evolving Agent Interfaces from task experience. A meta-agent examines task agents' trajectories on synthetic training tasks, without success labels, and constructs and revises interfaces and usage knowledge in a repository. Population-based evolution then selects which repositories to develop further by their performance on validation tasks the meta-agent never sees, favoring changes that generalize beyond the seen tasks. On OSWorld V2, Agent S4, with Qwen3.8-27B and the evolved repository of interfaces, sets a new state of the art in open-source computer-use agents, reaching 21.3% binary score, 3.8 times the same model with fixed interfaces. This is above both GPT-5.5 (13.0%) and Claude Opus 4.8 (20.6%), at about 4.3% and 1.5% of their respective costs. On ScienceBoard, the evolved interfaces improve the success rate from 41.4% to 58.6% with the same model. These results suggest that useful interfaces can be evolved from experience, making autonomous interface design a source of improvement complementary to advances in models and harnesses. We open-source our code at https://github.com/simular-ai/agent-s.

articles.title: LoWAgent: A Low-Resource Multilingual Benchmark for Web Agents
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27205v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Web agents are typically evaluated on English-language interfaces, leaving their ability to operate across the world's multilingual websites largely unexplored. This gap is especially significant for low-resource languages, where standardized resources for evaluating web agents remain limited. To address this gap, we introduce Low-Resource Web Agent Benchmark (LoWAgent), a benchmark for evaluating web agents across different low-resource languages (LRLs) in comparison to the default, English. LoWAgent evaluates web agents across English and four LRLs: Hindi, Bengali, Urdu, and Amharic. The benchmark comprises of six fully localized websites, instantiated across five languages to yield 3,000 task instances. We evaluate three closed-source and five open-source models across all five languages on all six websites. Our findings show that both closed-source and open-source models experience performance degradation for LRLs compared to English, with substantially greater performance drops observed among the open-source model agents. We further evaluate the robustness of the models on realistic interface disruptions, such as cookie notices and advertisement pop-ups, and find that these further degrade agentic performance. Finally, we show that post-training on a small subset of LoWAgent traces can significantly improve low-resource language agentic task performance, demonstrating the usefulness of our benchmark.

articles.title: AutoRedClaw: Automated Red-Teaming for Claw-Style Agents
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27244v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agent systems are shifting from task-scoped tool-use agents to persistent, personalized assistants such as OpenClaw. These claw-style agents maintain configuration files (e.g., AGENTS.md), long-term memory, and reusable skills. Once poisoned, this persistent state is repeatedly reloaded into the agent's context, creating persistent threats across tasks and sessions. Existing security evaluation systems struggle to evaluate these complex claw-style systems since they rely heavily on manually constructed test cases and environments, which limits their scale and coverage; in addition, these manually designed cases quickly become outdated as agents evolve, and their evaluation settings leave a gap with how claw-style agents are deployed in practice. To address this, we introduce AutoRedClaw, an automated red-teaming framework that generates end-to-end attacks together with the environments needed to execute them. AutoRedClaw combines a strict quality-checking protocol with execution-based validation to ensure the correctness, realism, and effectiveness of generated samples, and adopts task-driven environment construction to keep costs low. To achieve broad coverage, it organizes generation along risk categories, attack strategies, attack stages, and attack surfaces, and uses experience-guided exploration to steer generation toward under-explored regions. AutoRedClaw achieves an effective attack rate above 30% at less than 0.10 per successful sample. From its outputs, we construct RedClaw-Bench, a 330-case benchmark that yields substantially higher attack success rates (ASRs) than AgentDojo, AgentDyn, and DTap. Across seven harnesses and four frontier models, most agent systems exceed 50% ASR, showing that our red-teaming pipeline provides a strong evaluation signal even for the most advanced agent systems. Our code and benchmark are released at https://github.com/SaFo-Lab/AutoRedClaw.

articles.title: A Sustainable and Environmental-Friendly Acid-Reduced Route for Graphene Oxide Synthesis Through Modified Hummers Method
articles.abstract: The two-dimensional nanomaterial Graphene Oxide (GO) emerged as a cornerstone in materials science whose unique hydrophilic functional groups and tuneable physicochemical properties empower advanced applications in the fields of biomedicine, sensors, energy storage, catalysis etc. However, the Conventional Hummers Method for GO synthesis produces massive volumes of hazardous mineral acids waste, thereby presenting severe ecological hazards, complex wastewater management challenges and heightened operational safety risks related to exothermic reactions. Herein, we report a sustainable and green modification to the Hummers Method by suggesting an acid-sparse method for the preparation of GO, along with an effective oxidization of Graphite that has a reduced acid consumption. The modified protocol uses tailored synthetic parameters and a rate-controlled addition of the oxidant KMNO4 to facilitate the Synthesis of well-exfoliated GO with reduced use of acids and enhanced operational safety. A comprehensive characterization was done in order to confirm the efficient exfoliation, the successful oxidation

articles.title: Broadband Enhancement of Near-Field Radiative Heat Transfer via Intrinsic Carrier–Lattice Interactions
articles.abstract: In nanoscale semiconductor devices, heat dissipation is often limited by interfacial thermal resistance and structural discontinuities, where conventional phonon-mediated conduction becomes constrained. Although near-field radiative heat transfer (NFRHT) provides a non-contact pathway that can exceed the blackbody limit, it remains unclear how carrier dynamics and lattice vibrations jointly influence NFRHT in semiconductors. Here, we experimentally investigate NFRHT in the polar semiconductor gallium arsenide (GaAs) across different doping levels. By measuring the heat flux between macroscopic GaAs wafers separated by a 159 nm vacuum gap, we observe that heavily doped GaAs exhibits a 230% increase in heat transfer compared to its undoped counterpart, with the heat flux exceeding the blackbody limit by more than an order of magnitude. Combined fluctuational electrodynamics analysis and Raman spectroscopy indicate that this enhancement is associated with a coupled plasmonic-phononic response arising from intrinsic carrier-lattice interactions, leading to a broadened spectral distribution and enhanced thermal photons tunneling. These results reveal a link between carrier–lattice dynamics and near-field thermal radiation, providing insight into the development of tunable, non-contact thermal management strategies in nanoelectronic systems.

articles.title: Infrared Chemical Biopsy for Non-Destructive Compositional Assessment of Intact Bone
articles.abstract: Bone mechanical behavior reflects the integrated contributions of tissue composition and structure, yet compositional characterization generally requires tissue removal or specimen preparation. Here, we introduce Infrared Chemical Biopsy, a framework for non-destructive compositional interrogation of intact bone using fiber-optic near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy. As a proof-of-concept, we acquired NIR spectra directly from the lateral surface of the human ilium at a clinically relevant biopsy site before retrieving a spatially matched trephine transiliac biopsy. Intact-surface spectra contained characteristic features associated with bone water, collagen, mineral, and fat. The corresponding biopsy was subsequently characterized by micro-computed tomography and compression testing, establishing a sequential workflow linking intact-site compositional assessment with three-dimensional bone structure and mechanical behavior. Serial trimming of the biopsy from the medial surface, while maintaining the original lateral NIR measurement surface, produced systematic spectral changes as tissue thickness decreased, demonstrating that the intact-surface NIR signal contains contributions from underlying bone. These findings establish the feasibility of Infrared Chemical Biopsy as a spatially matched composition–structure–mechanics framework and provide a foundation for investigating bone quality non-destructively at accessible skeletal sites.

articles.title: The Smallest Standard Error Is the Wrong One: Selection Among Multiple Imputations Invalidates Inference
articles.abstract: Selecting, from M multiply imputed analyses, the candidate with the smallest estimated standard error looks like a precision-maximising choice. We show that it is systematically invalid. Minimum-standard-error selection discards the between-imputation variance that multiple imputation exists to capture and, by taking an order statistic, further depresses the reported within-imputation variance. The resulting standard error therefore does not estimate the sampling variability of the selected estimator. We formalise both mechanisms and show that selection can also bias the point estimate whenever candidate estimates and their estimated standard errors are dependent. A newly frozen, fully specified Monte Carlo implementation quantifies the effect. Under MAR with 30% missingness, n = 400 and M = 20, minimum-standard-error selection produced a calibration ratio of 0.77 and 84.5% coverage for nominal 95% intervals. Rubin pooling of the identical candidate draws restored the calibration ratio to 1.00 and coverage to 94.6%. In a 5,000-replication sweep, selection coverage declined monotonically from 86.7% at M = 2 to 81.7% at M = 100 while the magnitude of selection bias increased from 0.021 to 0.079; Rubin pooling remained approximately calibrated throughout. Two conclusions follow. First, an uncertainty estimate cannot simultaneously serve as an optimisation criterion and retain its usual inferential interpretation. Second, compare imputation procedures under a calibration-first protocol: establish that reported uncertainty tracks actual sampling variability before ranking methods by efficiency. We provide that protocol, a selection-corrected fallback, and a reproducibility archive from which we generate all revised numerical results.

articles.title: Composition-Time Verification of Resource-Constrained Quantum Subroutines in Digital Twin Workflows: A Visual Abstraction Approach
articles.abstract: Digital twin (DT) platforms for the built environment increasingly require computational capabilities that exceed classical resources, yet domain experts lack principled interfaces for incorporating quantum subroutines into their workflows. Existing visual quantum programming tools provide circuit-level composition but offer no domain-native constructs for DT data flows, while low-code quantum platforms abstract algorithm assembly without enforcing the resource constraints—ancilla budgets, uncomputation safety, and circuit depth—that determine whether a hybrid workflow is physically realizable. This paper presents a visual abstraction layer for composing quantum-classical hybrid workflows within DT environments, with a distinguishing emphasis on composition-time verification of resource constraints. The proposed three-tier architecture comprises: (1) a domain-native visual composition interface where users specify DT workflows using constructs such as sensor streams, simulation parameters, and optimization objectives; (2) an intermediate representation that lowers selected sub-tasks into reversible circuit specifications while statically checking ancilla availability, uncomputation existence, and depth budgets before execution; and (3) a provider-agnostic execution layer that dispatches verified subroutines to classical simulators or quantum backends and returns results to the visual layer. The central research question is whether resource constraints can be enforced at composition time rather than discovered at execution time, and what visual primitives are sufficient to express hybrid DT workflows without exposing gate-level details. We evaluate the approach through a realistic DT workload—building energy optimization with a quantum subroutine for combinatorial scheduling—measuring verification coverage, composition-time error detection rates, and usability with domain experts. The contribution is a verified abstraction layer that treats physical realizability as a first-class constraint in visual hybrid workflow design, addressing a gap at the intersection of DT systems, visual programming, and resource-aware quantum software engineering.

articles.title: A 2D discrete model with a phase-field regularisation applied to dynamic crack propagation
articles.abstract: In the current study, we propose a phase-field regularisation of a two-dimensional discrete model previously developed by the authors, with the aim of reducing the dependence of dynamic crack propagation on the orientation of the lattice. The proposed model combines first-neighbour normal and transverse bond interactions with a nodal phase field calibrated with the tensile strength and the fracture energy. The gradient energy is expressed as a sum over the lattice bonds, and the equations of motion are integrated explicitly. Three numerical examples are analysed: the Kalthoff–Winkler test, a single-edge-notched plate under tension and the fragmentation of a thick cylinder under internal impulsive pressure. The first two tests are studied on lattices rotated by 0, 15 and 30 degrees, while centred and shifted lattices are considered for the cylinder. The results are presented in terms of the crack path, the propagation speed, the load–displacement response and the energies, and are compared with experimental observations and numerical results reported in the literature. The regularisation reduces the directional bias in the Kalthoff–Winkler and tension tests, while the cylinder illustrates the influence of lattice symmetry and regularisation on fragmentation. The differences between the energy removed by bond degradation and the regularised crack energy are also discussed.

articles.title: Modeling of frozen rocks thawing around an injection well during water-polymer flooding of a gas-oil stratum
articles.abstract: The conjugate problem of the thermal effect of an injection well on permafrost rocks during the injection of a water-polymer solution into a gas-oil stratum to enhance oil recovery is considered. Within the framework of a quasi-stationary flow model in the well and an axisymmetric heat transfer model in rocks, the thawing dynamics in the permafrost zone is assessed. When constructing the computational algorithm, the significant difference in time scales for processes occurring in the well and in the rocks was taken into account. For the numerical solution of the Stefan problem, a level set method with smoothed functions of thermophysical coefficients and an algorithm for implementing the simple iteration method are used. It has been shown that the well rate and the temperature of the solution at the wellhead exert the primary influence on the dynamics of rock temperature field formation and the thawing of frozen rock. However, at high solution temperatures, the thawing radius at the base of frozen rocks, as well as near the surface, will be significant, which for wells in unconsolidated rocks may pose a certain danger to surface equipment.

articles.title: Evidence of climate warming in Iberian caves
articles.abstract: Caves are generally regarded as thermally stable and climatically buffered environments, yet their temperatures can respond to long-term surface changes. We tested whether subterranean warming reflects the accelerated climate change affecting Western Europe, using high-resolution temperature records from two caves in the Western Iberian Peninsula: Vale Telheiro and Algar do Pena. Cave records were compared with surface climatic variables, and temporal trends evaluated using Mann-Kendall tests and Sen’s slope estimators. Both caves evidenced significant warming, but with different relationships with surface climatic variables. Vale Telheiro warmed approximately 0.111°C year⁻¹, while the surface trend was weaker and not statistically significant; temperatures followed inverse seasonal cycles, with a lag of approximately five months. Algar do Pena warmed approximately 0.053°C year⁻¹, while surface temperature increased more rapidly. This cave showed stronger seasonal coupling and a shorter delay (approximately two months). These patterns demonstrate that cave warming does not simply reproduce the magnitude or timing of surface warming. Instead, cave-specific thermal buffering, ventilation, hydrology and heat-transfer processes seem to determine how regional climate change is expressed underground. Our findings extend evidence of cave warming to southwestern European karsts, highlighting the importance of long-term monitoring for anticipating impacts on thermally sensitive subterranean ecosystems.

articles.title: Development of a voltage-divider based probe method for sheet resistance measurement of copper foils and thin films
articles.abstract: Accurate measurement of sheet resistance is essential for the electrical characterization of thin metallic films and foils, particularly when sample dimensions and thickness approach the limits of conventional probe-based techniques. A voltage-divider-based probe method was developed for measuring the sheet resistance of copper samples over micrometer- and nanometer-scale thicknesses. The proposed system combines a controlled electrical measurement circuit with a digital data-acquisition unit and was designed to reduce the sensitivity of the measurement to probe spacing and sample geometry under defined dimensional conditions. Copper foils with thicknesses from 20 to 100 µm and thermally evaporated copper films with thicknesses of approximately 32–529 nm were investigated. The sheet resistance and electrical resistivity obtained using the proposed method were compared with measurements performed using a conventional four-point probe. For micrometer-thick copper foils, the two methods produced closely comparable resistivity values, indicating good agreement between the proposed method and the four-point-probe measurements under the experimental conditions used. At the nanometer scale, the proposed method remained capable of measuring samples thinner than 100 nm, for which the four-point probe measurements were not obtained under the experimental conditions used in this study. The measured resistivity increased with decreasing film thickness, consistent with enhanced electron scattering associated with size-dependent transport. The results demonstrate that the proposed voltage-divider-based method can provide a simple and reproducible approach for sheet-resistance characterization of small copper foils and thin films, while its applicability to ultrathin and non-uniform samples should be considered within the assumptions of the measurement model.

articles.title: Response Surface Methodology Optimization of Multi-Metal Adsorption onto Fika Bentonite Clay Using Box-Behnken Design
articles.abstract: This study employed response surface methodology (RSM) with a Box-Behnken design (BBD) to optimize the adsorption of five heavy metals (Cu, Pb, Fe, Co, As) onto Nigerian Fika bentonite clay. Twenty-nine experimental runs were conducted to evaluate the effects of four independent factors: pH (2–12), adsorbent dosage (0.1–0.5 g/L), initial metal concentration (10–50 mg/L), and contact time (20–120 min). Quadratic response surface models were developed for each metal using Design Expert software (version 6.0). Analysis of variance (ANOVA) revealed that all models were statistically significant (p < 0.05). For copper, the model F-value was 7.35 (p = 0.0003) with R² = 0.8803. Significant model terms included adsorbent dosage (B), initial concentration (C), the quadratic term B², and interactions BC (dosage × concentration) and BD (dosage × time). For lead, the model was highly significant (F = 11.72, p < 0.0001, R² = 0.9214). Iron, cobalt, and arsenic models were also highly significant (F = 43.40, 43.37, and 43.41 respectively; R² = 0.9775, 0.9775, and 0.9775 respectively). The interaction between adsorbent dosage and initial concentration (BC) was significant for all five metals, confirming the importance of optimizing these parameters simultaneously. The global optimum conditions identified were pH 7, adsorbent dosage 0.30 g/L, initial concentration 30 mg/L, and contact time 70 min. Confirmatory experiments at these conditions gave adsorption capacities of 1.18 mg/g (Cu), 1.15 mg/g (Pb), 1.19 mg/g (Fe), 1.21 mg/g (Co), and 0.61 mg/g (As), all within 95% prediction intervals. The adequate precision ratios ranged from 11.99 to 26.83, all above the threshold of 4, indicating that the models can be used to navigate the design space. These results demonstrate that Fika bentonite, particularly in its raw form, is a promising cost-effective adsorbent for multi-metal wastewater treatment.

articles.title: Characterization and archived CO₂ hydrogenation data for bimetallic catalysts on octahedral ceria
articles.abstract: CO₂ hydrogenation can yield carbon monoxide through reverse water-gas shift or methane through methanation, making reliable sample provenance and carbon accounting essential for catalyst comparison. This work examines octahedral CeO₂-supported CuNi, FeCu, and AuRu formulations using available characterization and archived catalytic records. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) shows faceted ceria particles, while energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) supports local Cu/Ni and Fe/Cu co-presence. AuRu elemental quantification differs between the archived report and manuscript figure. The archived summary suggests temperature-dependent differences in normalized CO/CH₄ distributions, with CuNi- and FeCu-labelled series relatively CO-rich at elevated temperature and an AuRu-labelled series showing a methane-rich interval. Sample-to-run links, conversion scaling, and catalyst-mass/flow bases remain unresolved. Recalculation repairs a recoverable carbon-product denominator error and includes recorded C₂/C₃ products, but does not establish sample identity or independent inlet–outlet carbon closure.

articles.title: A polarized charge model for RNA: enhanced stability of G- quadruplexes and improved folding free energy landscapes
articles.abstract: Ribonucleic acid (RNA) plays essential roles in numerous biological processes, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations have become indispensable for probing RNA structure and function at atomic resolution. However, current RNA force fields exhibit notable deficiencies in describing hydrogen bonding, ion stability, and folding pathways, largely because they neglect the electrostatic screening effect of aqueous solvent. To address these limitations, we introduce a set of polarized nucleic acid-specific charges (PNC) derived from fragment-based quantum chemistry calculations and apply them to two representative RNA systems. The PNC method explicitly incorporates polarization effects into electrostatic interactions. For the G-quadruplex (GQ) system, PNC appreciably enhances structural stability, particularly by preserving hydrogen bonds between G-tetrads, and retains cations within the central channel across nearly all tested ion models. In contrast, standard AMBER force fields without polarization allow terminal cations to escape into bulk solvent within a few nanoseconds. For folding of a single-stranded RNA into a hairpin motif, none of the five conventional AMBER force fields yields a physically reasonable free-energy landscape, whereas four show clear improvement when combined with PNC. Despite its structural dependence—a recognized limitation—the PNC method offers excellent compatibility: it requires no modification to the original force-field functional form and incurs no additional computational cost, making it a practical and efficient tool for RNA simulations

articles.title: Uncovering Physiological Responses of Idesia polycarpa 'Yuji' Under Alkali Stress via Transcriptomics
articles.abstract: This study aimed to investigate the growth, physiological, and molecular responses of Idesia polycarpa ‘Yuji’ under different intensities of alkali stress, thereby providing a theoretical basis for its wider cultivation and application in saline-alkali areas. Two-year-old I. polycarpa ‘Yuji’ seedlings were used in a pot experiment. A mixed alkali stress solution of NaHCO₃:Na₂CO₃ = 9:1 molar ratio was applied at three concentration gradients: J1, 60 mmol·L− 1 ; J2, 90 mmol·L− 1; and J3, 120 mmol·L− 1. Deionized water was used as the control treatment (CK). Our integrated analysis revealed that I. polycarpa ‘Yuji’ exhibited heightened sensitivity during the later stages of alkali stress, which progressively inhibited growth, damaged the microstructure of leaves and root tips, and severely impaired photosynthetic function, as evidenced by reduced pigment content and decreased net photosynthetic and transpiration rates. Physiological analysis revealed that as stress intensity and duration increased, soluble sugars (SS), soluble proteins (SP), proline (Pro) accumulated significantly, while malondialdehyde (MDA) content rose continuously, indicating severe oxidative damage to the cell membrane system. Peroxidase (POD) and superoxide dismutase (SOD) activities showing distinct activation patterns. Hormonal analysis revealed that under J1 to J2 stress, abscisic acid (ABA) levels fluctuated, while indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), zeatin riboside (ZR), and gibberellic acid-3 (GA₃) levels increased, whereas under J3 stress they were suppressed. A total of 9,995 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified in the transcriptome sequencing of the control group (CK) and the J3 group. KEGG enrichment analysis revealed that DEGs were significantly enriched in pathways such as photosynthesis-antenna proteins. Transcriptome analysis identified 9 995 DEGs. KEGG enrichment analysis indicated that photosynthesis-antenna proteins, photosynthesis, and the plant MAPK signaling pathway played key roles in the response to alkali stress. In addition, hormone signal transduction-related genes, including ARR, ABF, PYR/PYL, and AHP, were significantly DEGs. This study clarified the physiological and molecular mechanisms underlying alkali tolerance in I. polycarpa ‘Yuji’ and identified candidate genes and key metabolic pathways associated with alkali stress resistance. These findings provide a theoretical foundation and genetic resources for stress-resistance improvement, efficient utilization of saline-alkali land, and the large-scale cultivation of this tree species.

articles.title: Activation-Grade-Scheduled Predictive Control for Battery–Supercapacitor Electric-Vehicle Energy Management
articles.abstract: Battery–supercapacitor hybrid energy storage systems can buffer traction transients, but predictive power sharing must balance battery loading, DC-link regulation, and supercapacitor reserve. We develop an activation-grade-scheduled predictive controller (M5) that adjusts penalties on battery current, current variation, DC-link voltage error, and supercapacitor energy using bounded operating-condition indicators. A deterministic coarse-to-fine scalar search selects the battery power command over a ten-step horizon; a soft terminal-energy term discourages systematic reserve depletion. A separate M3–M5 comparison examines battery stress and terminal energy fairness against conventional fixed-weight predictive control. We then evaluate a candidate-screened extension (M6) that excludes predicted trajectories outside an internal supercapacitor operating interval when admissible candidates exist. Both controllers are tested on matched WLTP and UDDS speed traces from an initial supercapacitor voltage of 267 V, using the same nominal simulation plant. M6 reduced post-step samples below the operating state-of-charge threshold of 0.08 from 963 to zero under WLTP and from 49 to zero under UDDS. However, battery-current root-mean-square increased from 19.229 to 19.426 A and from 10.598 to 10.816 A, respectively. DC-link voltage root-mean-square error increased from 0.334 to 0.461 V and from 0.306 to 0.420 V. Terminal supercapacitor energy changes remained similar within each paired test. These results identify an operating-reserve versus electrical-performance trade-off rather than an across-the-board improvement. Because the screening margin is heuristic, the prediction and plant models differ, and an unscreened fallback remains possible, the observed nominal behavior does not establish robust constraint satisfaction. Independent cycles, model uncertainty, repeated noise trials, and hardware-in-the-loop validation are needed.

articles.title: Effective band structure control for single-atom-thick arsenic chain via strain manipulation by single-walled carbon nanotubes
articles.abstract: Strain manipulation in low-dimensional material provides the chance to effectively and accurately modify their electronic and optoelectronic properties. Here, we synthesized small-diameter single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) filled with the group V element arsenic (As) and discovered different crystal phases in SWCNTs with a narrow diameter distribution (0.80 < dt < 0.91 nm). Gel permeation chromatography (GPC) was then applied for purification of as-filled SWCNTs by chirality, enabling an efficient enrichment of one-dimensional (1D) asymmetric zigzag As-based chains within the inner cavity of (7,5) and (8,4) SWNCTs. Photoluminescence and pressure-dependent Raman spectroscopic measurements were used as complementary tools to probe radial strain in these 1D heterostructures. In essence, pressure-dependent Raman measurements up to a medium-high pressure (~ 10 GPa) reveal that both metallic and semiconducting SWCNTs exhibit unconventional Raman mode frequency shifts and Raman intensity changes after filling, which was associated with abnormal lattice dynamics under pressure. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that asymmetric zigzag chains can transition from metallic to direct-bandgap semiconducting chains under certain compressive strain, likely due to the structure evolution of π-like valence bands. The large tunability of electronic bands together with clear knowledge of the local environment offer a useful platform for investigating strongly correlated electron states within 1D systems.

articles.title: A Hybrid TFT-NBEATS Framework for Robust Multi-Horizon Photovoltaic Power Forecasting
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27155v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate multi-horizon photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting is essential for grid stability, energy scheduling, and the efficient operation of PVbatterygrid systems. However, existing models often fail to jointly capture short-term variability and long-term temporal patterns, while lacking unified multi-horizon capability and interpretability. To address these limitations, this study proposes a novel hybrid deep learning framework that integrates a Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) and N-BEATS within an attention-based fusion architecture. The proposed model leverages TFT to learn short-term temporal dependencies and dynamic feature importance, while N-BEATS captures long-term trend and seasonal components through interpretable basis decomposition. An adaptive attention mechanism dynamically fuses both branches, enabling balanced multi-scale learning. The framework simultaneously generates forecasts for 30-minute, 2-hour, 6-hour, 12-hour, and 24-hour horizons within a single unified pipeline. The model is evaluated using multi-year real-world datasets from the Desert Knowledge Australia Solar Centre (DKASC). Experimental results demonstrate superior performance over statistical, machine learning, and deep learning baselines. The proposed model achieves RMSE values of 42.35, 46.27, 52.29, and 48.11 across the 20162017, 2023, 2024, and 20252026 datasets, respectively, corresponding to a 3540% reduction compared to the best baseline (TFT). Additionally, MAPE remains below 5% across all datasets, indicating high predictive accuracy and stability. The model also provides interpretability through attention visualization and trendseasonality decomposition, and is deployed on a cloud-based platform for real-time forecasting. These results demonstrate that the proposed framework is robust, interpretable, and suitable for practical renewable energy applications.

articles.title: Decision Sufficiency of Learned Representation Interfaces for Safe Generative Control
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27446v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A controller can guide a language model toward safe and useful responses by choosing when to assist, ask for clarification, or refuse. When the controller uses selected internal features, poor performance alone cannot distinguish missing information from limitations of its decision rules or training. We study decision sufficiency: whether the best controller using a representation can match the minimum average loss attainable with full state information, under the same strategies and evaluation criteria. For interfaces with finitely many outputs, we compute the optimal loss exactly and separate the three sources of excess loss. Pairwise checks can miss information loss: states with the same controller input may share an optimal strategy in every pair but not across the whole group. We bound the number of states needed to reveal a conflict and characterize the fewest outputs an unrestricted interface needs to avoid all conflicts. We audit selected features from sparse autoencoders, which encode model activations using relatively few active features, in Qwen2.5, SmolLM2, and Phi. On SmolLM2 responses scored by two human raters, restricting the controller to two selected on/off features increases its minimum average loss by 0.0345--0.1166 relative to full state information, even with the governing policy supplied. Both independently trained autoencoders show the increase on both evaluation sets. The audit identifies decision failures that require changing the controller's input, not merely its architecture or training.

articles.title: TRCM: Topology-Aware Route-Consistency Modeling for Robust Neural Vehicle Routing
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27568v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural combinatorial optimization has enabled fast constructive solvers for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP), yet most autoregressive models still construct solutions through sequential node selection and represent route organization only implicitly. We investigate whether route-level customer co-assignment can be modeled explicitly and used to guide this node-level decision process. To this end, we propose TopologyAware RouteConsistency Modeling (TRCM), which reuses node representations from a standard autoregressive construction pipeline to predict pairwise same-route probabilities and injects them into customer selection as a route-consistency signal. Because sameroute supervision is both class-imbalanced and structurally uneven, TRCM combines structure-preserving augmentation with Topological Entropy (TE)- based reweighting to emphasize locally ambiguous customer pairs. Under matched decoding budgets, TRCM reduces the optimality gap from 3.67% to 3.28% on CVRP50 and from 2.11% to 1.99% on CVRP100; under 8-fold augmented inference, it reduces the CVRP100 gap from 1.61% to 1.49%. On XML100, TRCM*8Aug improves the average objective by 0.24%, with larger gains on several structurally informative factors. A controlled demand-reassignment test over 500 variants further shows more concentrated objective fluctuations. These results support explicit route-consistency modeling as an effective structural principle for autoregressive neural routing.

articles.title: Learning Inter-Graph Interactions Between Heterogeneous Substructures of Chemical Systems
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27614v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Complex chemical systems containing heterogeneous substructures are common in real-world applications. Various physical phenomena of the complex chemical systems are derived from the interactions between the heterogeneous substructures. However, existing graph representation learning methods for inter-graph interactions assumed graph-level interactions between homogeneous structures, such as organic molecules and inorganic crystalline materials. We propose a data descriptor of the complex chemical systems and a graph neural network for learning inter-graph interactions between organic and inorganic compounds. We applied the proposed method to predict the physical properties of hybrid solar cell materials containing heterogeneous substructures, which have received significant attention for sustainable energy resources. By learning heterogeneous inter-graph interactions, the proposed method achieved state-of-the-art accuracy in predicting band gaps of 1,682 hybrid solar cell materials.

articles.title: Foundation-Style Pretraining for Scalable and Transferable Distributed PV Forecasting
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27763v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid growth of distributed photovoltaic (PV) generation is increasing the demand for accurate forecasting across large numbers of geographically dispersed stations. Existing approaches are commonly developed for individual sites or specific forecasting horizons, requiring repeated training and maintenance as new stations are integrated and limiting direct reuse at previously unseen sites. To address this scalability gap, this paper presents a domain-specific foundation-style pretraining framework that learns a shared forecasting model from heterogeneous multi-site and multi-horizon PV data. NWP-assisted forecasting is formulated as a sequence-completion problem that unifies historical PV power, meteorological observations, future numerical weather prediction (NWP) forecasts, and time encodings. Three pretraining objectives are designed and systematically evaluated, including forecast-aligned reconstruction, generic reconstruction, and mixed reconstruction. The mixed objective combines the operational structure of PV forecasting with random sequence reconstruction and provides the most balanced performance across forecasting accuracy, degraded NWP conditions, and downstream adaptation. Experiments on 479 distributed PV stations use 340 stations for model development and 139 spatially held-out stations for zero-shot evaluation. Across horizons from 6 hours to 7 days, the multi-site pretrained MR model outperforms representative station-specific and shared baselines, as well as generalist time-series models, including a recent large-scale pretrained foundation model. The pretrained model can also be directly deployed at new PV stations and subsequently adapted to region-specific operational objectives when local data become available, providing a scalable forecasting paradigm for large distributed PV fleets.

articles.title: From Generic to Dedicated: A Novel Optimizer for Online Continual Learning
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Online Continual Learning (OCL) requires models to learn from non-stationary data streams under a strict single-pass constraint, making them highly susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. While existing studies have explored various strategies from data, architecture, and optimization perspectives, the optimizer often directly uses generic approaches such as SGD and AdamW. In this work, we reveal a new link between optimization dynamics and OCL needs by recasting Polyak-Ruppert averaging as the engine of "plasticity" and Primal averaging as the anchor of "stability". This inspires our novel optimizer, SPIN (Stability-Plasticity INterpolation), which explicitly decouples plasticity and stability by interpolating between a fast-moving "plasticity" sequence and an adaptive "stability" sequence. We theoretically demonstrate that SPIN implicitly employs an inverse Hessian approximation, providing crucial Tikhonov regularization to damp noisy, single-sample Hessian estimates and mitigate forgetting. More importantly, SPIN can be seamlessly integrated into existing OCL methods by taking resulted gradients as input and replacing standard optimizers. Extensive experiments show that using SPIN instead of standard optimizers yields consistent and significant performance gains across multiple OCL approaches, including the challenging rehearsal-free setting and under strict memory constraints.

articles.title: Geometry-Agnostic Data-Driven Discovery of Extreme Scenarios
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.28487v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a two-stage data-driven neural framework for discovering dynamically admissible extreme scenarios. Rather than assuming prior knowledge of the governing equations, the first stage infers the effective dynamical constraints directly from observational data. When the underlying physical system possesses suitable symmetries, the learned dynamics can be represented in a geometry-agnostic form, independent of any fixed grid, coordinate system, dimensionality, and intrinsic curvature. In the second stage, a physics-informed neural-search uses this learned dynamics to uncover rare, high-impact coherent structures that may not have appeared in the original observations. We demonstrate this framework through representative examples of increasing dimensionality and geometric complexity. Starting from a traditionally learned Duffing dynamics, we find a homoclinic pulse as a plausible localized extreme scenario. Next, since the same equation also appears in the stationary nonlinear Schrodinger system, with the coordinate interpreted as space instead of time, this pulse becomes a standing soliton. We then retrain the first stage using a geometry-agnostic neural representation, enabling the learned dynamics to be lifted to higher-dimensional space to obtain higher-dimensional solitary profile, known as Townes soliton. Finally, with a Liouville system, we demonstrate that dynamics learned from data on a (1+1)-dimensional Lorentzian quasi-manifold can be transferred to a (2+0)-dimensional Euclidean manifold to identify an instanton. Our approach can be applied to other coherent spatiotemporal structures, including kinks, rogue waves, compactons, peakons, and potentially even singularities, with applications in risk analysis, nonlinear forecasting, and anomaly detection.

articles.title: PaPi: Parallel Picard-Duhamel Integration for Fast Neuro-Spectral Architectures
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.28591v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neuro-spectral architectures (NeuSA) are a class of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) that have proven effective for solving time-dependent PDEs in the frequency domain. However, training and inference often rely on costly numerical integration of the learned vector field, typically using sequential Runge-Kutta time stepping, which limits temporal parallelism. We introduce PaPi, an integration scheme inspired by weakly nonlinear flows that enables time-Parallel inference through exponential integration and a Duhamel-Picard scheme. We show that the Duhamel-Picard iteration converges exponentially for all flows, and provide explicit error bounds that depend on how close the flow is to linear. Experiments show that PaPi accelerates training and inference by up to two orders of magnitude, achieving training times of under one second for low-dimensional PDE learning problems, while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy.

articles.title: Planning under Noise with Neural Operators
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.28623v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: Planning under uncertain control execution noise requires reliable feedback policies across diverse environments. We introduce Planning Under Noise (PUN), a neural operator that learns noise-aware value fields for planning in unseen geometries. Building on an established screened-Poisson formulation of stochastic optimal control, we address two challenges: specifying boundary conditions that support navigation across varying geometries and efficiently computing fields with reliable gradients. Zero-Dirichlet obstacle boundaries terminate sampled paths at walls, weakening the goal signal along long routes and making it harder to estimate reliably. We instead impose reflecting Neumann conditions on obstacles and a Dirichlet condition at the goal, allowing sampled paths to continue exploring free space until they reach the target. To solve the resulting PDE without a configuration-space mesh, we extend a Monte Carlo (MC) solver, Walk on Stars (WoSt), to higher dimensions. However, local MC fluctuations can reverse estimated gradient directions and cause planning failures, making direct planning require costly sampling. PUN amortizes this computation by learning geometry-to-field mappings from noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo labels, avoiding expensive convergence for every training example. At inference, test-time scaling uses bounded local search guided by the predicted global field. We evaluate PUN on planning tasks across dimensions. Across four noise levels, PUN matches or outperforms all compared planners, achieving 95-100% success on the 4D replanning benchmark while maintaining the lowest runtime. At the highest tested noise level in 4D, PUN achieves 10.7-60.6% relative gains in success rate over other methods while running 3.29-32.15 times faster.

articles.title: This is SParTA: A modular, efficient and scalable transformer architecture for jet-tagging
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27106v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present the Sparse Particle-interaction Transformer Architecture (SParTA), a modular, scalable, and efficient transformer for jet tagging at high-energy colliders. Exploiting the steeply falling transverse-momentum (p_T) spectrum of jet constituents, SParTA factorizes constituent processing into two topological regimes. Ordered by descending p_T, only the N hardest constituents (the hard core) participate in quadratic O(N²) differential interaction attention driven by pairwise physical and learned relational features. The remaining soft constituents are integrated via linear O(lN) cross-attention to the hard core, preserving soft-radiation and color-flow information while avoiding the O(l²) memory bottleneck of full self-attention over all l constituents. Pairwise interaction features are computed dynamically in-network from constituent four-momenta and conditioned on global jet-level substructure observables. On the quark-gluon tagging benchmark, a 300K-parameter SParTA model achieves an AUC of 92.02% and accuracy of 85.06%, matching the 2.14M-parameter Particle Transformer (ParT) at one-seventh the parameter count and outperforming IAFormer by 21% in background rejection at 30% signal efficiency. On the boosted top-tagging benchmark, SParTA outperforms ParT and ParticleNet with 511K parameters, while we analyze the architectural trade-offs relative to fully dense multi-layer interaction networks.

articles.title: Towards Interaction State Recognition in Sensorized Gecko-Inspired Adhesive Interfaces for Orbital Servicing
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27141v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reliable contact establishment remains a critical challenge for autonomous on-orbit servicing (OOS), particularly when interacting with non-cooperative targets. Gecko-inspired dry adhesives provide a lightweight, passive, and residue-free solution for robotic capture in space, yet current systems operate in open loop, without the ability to estimate their own contact or adhesion state during interaction. This paper presents a real-time interaction-awareness framework that enables sensorized gecko-inspired adhesive interfaces to estimate their contact state throughout the adhesion lifecycle using embedded capacitive sensing. Five discrete interaction states (idle, proximity, contact, engaged, and disengaged) are classified using experimentally collected and augmented sensor data, enabling a comparative evaluation of six lightweight machine learning models suitable for embedded deployment. Among the evaluated models, Random Forest achieved the highest offline classification accuracy of 95.65%. For online deployment, combining Random Forest with a rule-based state machine improved accuracy from 78.02% to 93.14%, achieving a macro F1-score of 0.9343 while maintaining a 53 ms inference cycle. These results demonstrate that incorporating physics-consistent state constraints significantly improves robustness during realtime inference, representing a step toward interaction-aware capture in future autonomous orbital servicing missions.

articles.title: Low Residuals, Wrong Value: Learning the Viscosity Solution of Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs Equations with PINNs
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27193v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and other residual-trained solvers judge a candidate solution by the size of its sampled PDE residual. For first-order Hamilton-Jacobi equations this is not sufficient: the same equation and boundary data admit Lipschitz almost-everywhere solutions that differ from the viscosity solution by O(1) while violating the equation only on sets of measure zero. We study whether residual minimization selects such solutions in a fixed-horizon pursuit-evasion game whose Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs value function is known in closed form on the circle S¹ and on the flat tori T² and T⁴. We train four neural parameterizations with ten seeds on each geometry, 120 runs in total. A standard network with periodic Fourier features converges to folded almost-everywhere solutions in all 30 runs: small residuals and the expected capture-layer gradient, yet values that are wrong over most of the domain. A network with periodicity imposed through the loss recovers the viscosity solution in one and two dimensions but becomes unreliable in four. Two parameterizations that receive the geodesic distance do substantially better: a single network fed the wrapped displacement and its distance recovers the viscosity solution in all 30 runs, while a minimum over periodic image charts succeeds in 27 of 30 and introduces a wrong-image failure mode. Finally, for the convex Hamiltonian considered here, we use the semiconcavity of the viscosity solution to build a mesh-free finite-difference test that needs only forward network evaluations; it detects the folded solutions and the harmful min-of-charts failures without access to the exact value function. A small sampled residual thus does not by itself validate a learned Hamilton-Jacobi solution; the parameterization and independent structural diagnostics can be essential for selecting the viscosity solution.

articles.title: EMBER: Predicting TCR--pMHC Binding Without a Docked Complex
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27334v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose EMBER, a structure-based framework for TCR--pMHC binding prediction that eliminates the need for a predicted docked complex, and with it the placement error that dominates such predictions. Traditional structure-based predictors utilize the co-folded complex structure of the receptor and the antigen and interpret binding from its contact surface. Consequently, every downstream feature inherits any deviation the structure-prediction tool introduced. Methodologically, EMBER folds the TCR and pMHC independently, encodes them as SE(3)-invariant residue graphs, and compares their learned representations without constructing a shared coordinate frame. A relative pose is therefore not an input of the model, so placement error cannot propagate into the prediction. Computationally, EMBER preprocesses O(N+M) monomer folds where a complex-based predictor needs O(NM) operations. Experimentally, under epitope-disjoint evaluation with six retrained baselines, EMBER is first on every metric under all four folding tools, by 0.9 to 14.4% in micro-AUROC, 18.5 to 25.3% in micro-AUPRC and 10.6 to 24.1% in MCC. Its ranking is also up to 85% more stable across folding tools.

articles.title: Soliton Profiles in 1D: Enhanced Neural-Network Solvers and Constrained Deep Ritz Methods
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27500v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop and compare enhanced neural-network solvers for one-dimensional ground-state profiles, which are solutions of  Qprⁱmeprⁱme=bQ-γ Qp,quad Q>0,quad p>1, quad b, γ >0,  the stationary profile equation for the nonlinear Schrödinger, generalized Korteweg-de Vries, and nonlinear Klein-Gordon equations. Its explicit sech-type solutions serve as exact reference for error computation and benchmark hyperparameter selection. We improve on the standard Adam-trained physics-informed neural network (PINN) baseline by introducing higher-order optimization via Gauss-Newton/Levenberg-Marquardt and L-BFGS refinements, as well as Fourier-feature PINNs, and constrained Deep Ritz (DR) formulations. In DR approaches we introduce two new neural-network formulations, which implement two classical variational characterizations: a Nehari-constrained Deep Ritz method, in which the height is learned by projecting onto the Nehari/Pokhozhaev manifold, and a Weinstein Deep Ritz method, in which a normalized profile minimizes the Weinstein quotient. The Deep Ritz formulations perform best overall, in particular, the Weinstein variant gives the best error-runtime balance. The neural-network based solvers remain less accurate and efficient than classical Petviashvili iteration in 1D, however, the current study provides a proof of concept: the mesh-free formulation, non-reliance on exact profiles or the related features make them promising in higher dimensions and for more complicated nonlinearities and dispersive operators.

articles.title: Factual Access States in Diffusion Language Models: From Mechanism to Knowledge Editing and Retrieval
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27580v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Factual recall is a lookup: some representation inside the network serves as the key, and what that key is made of decides which queries can retrieve the fact, what an edit must cover, and what a retriever can read. We call it the factual access state. In autoregressive (AR) models the subject position enriches attributes largely independently of the relation, and relation-specific selection happens later, at the readout position. In masked diffusion language models (DLMs) we find the state is assembled differently, and much earlier: in the first attention layer the wording of the relation is routed into the position of whichever entity is visible and the early feed-forward layers look the fact up on this fused representation. The state therefore varies with the relation's surface form and with the query direction, so the queries about one fact occupy a region of state space rather than a point, and an operation on the fact succeeds only for queries that enter it. We treat the state as an interface to a DLM's factual knowledge, and put it to two uses. Writing to the state gives a knowledge editor: from one declarative statement, Multi-View Edit fits one shared value per direction across that region and installs it in the early-MLP block, preserving source-prompt reliability while substantially improving paraphrase and reverse question answering, where AR editors gain near zero. Reading it suggests a complementary use: the state at each entity position can serve as a relation-specific retrieval vector with no training, returning both pieces of evidence for two-entity queries on which pooled, prompted and lexical retrievers almost never return both.

articles.title: You Are the Trigger: Speaker-Activated Backdoors
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.27210v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speech models are increasingly used as an interface to AI systems, from transcription tools to voice agents. Existing audio backdoors require an attacker to introduce triggers at inference time. We study a different threat model in which the attacker compromises the model during fine-tuning but has no access to the victim's inference-time inputs. We introduce the Speaker-Activated Backdoor (SAB) setting, in which a target speaker's natural voice serves as the trigger. We develop a two-phase fine-tuning method that first makes speaker identity more accessible and then binds the target speaker to an attacker-chosen payload. Compared with a one-phase baseline with the same training budget, the two-phase method substantially improves selectivity and clean performance, and is especially important for content-dependent attacks. SAB achieves 90.2% and 97.0% backdoor success on Whisper-medium and Parakeet, with false-positive rates of 1.7% and 0%, respectively using as little as two minutes of real audio from the target speaker. We further demonstrate content-dependent semantic rewriting and downstream tool-use attacks, where malicious instructions are inserted into 96.9% of target-speaker transcripts. When these transcripts are passed to frontier LLM agents, GPT-4o and Claude (Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku), the injected instruction drives the agent to carry out the harmful action in up to 87.5% of cases. The attack generalizes to held-out recordings, multiple target speakers, and common acoustic degradations. These results establish speaker identity as a practical backdoor trigger that requires no inference-time attacker access and is invisible at the transcript layer.

articles.title: Rise, fall, and rebirth of an oxide: Growth and evolution of bismuth oxide on Au(111)
articles.abstract: Author(s): Alberto Turoldo, Marco Bianchi, Deborah Perco, Andrea Berti, Philip Hofmann, Alessandro Baraldi, and Silvano Lizzit The authors report a comprehensive, multitechnique study of bismuth oxide growth on Au(111) under varying temperatures and oxygen exposures. Combining synchrotron-based spectroscopy, diffraction, and scanning tunneling microscopy, they elucidate the structural evolution during oxidation and annealing. Oxidation produces multiple oxide domains, including a structure consistent with the (201) surface of β-Bi 2 O 3 , while annealing drives phase separation and Au redistribution to the oxide surface. These processes induce substantial electronic modifications and lower the work function to 3.4 eV, highlighting the potential of Bi 2 O 3 as a low-work-function interlayer for contact engineering in two-dimensional semiconductor devices. articles.title: Second-order magnetic properties in paramagnetic molecules from a current density formulation including scalar relativistic effects
articles.abstract: This work presents the theoretical background for the computation of nuclear magnetic shielding, nuclear hyperfine, and magnetizability tensors of paramagnetic molecules using a magnetically induced current density framework to account for both orbital and spin contributions. The resulting magnetizability tensor is fully consistent with the general Van Vleck formulation, recovering the temperature-dependent Curie contribution through the explicit integration of the magnetically induced spin current density. The methodology proposed herein provides a straightforward computational route that bypasses the complex evaluation of g-tensors and zero-field splitting Hamiltonians. While the theoretical framework is general, we present applications rooted in physically motivated approximations where scalar relativistic effects are incorporated through corrections based on the zeroth-order regular approximation Hamiltonian within the ground-state spin density. This approach combines a relativistic self-consistent field calculation for the ground-state spin density with a non-relativistic, origin-independent current density calculation for the orbital contribution. This hybrid strategy is shown to capture the heavy-atom light-atom effect in 1 H and 13 C shieldings, particularly in paramagnetic molecular systems containing transition metals up to the 3d series. By restricting the relativistic treatment to the spin density, where scalar relativistic effects are dominant, and neglecting such effects on the orbital contribution of light atoms, this method offers a good compromise between computational efficiency and accuracy for the characterization of large open-shell molecular systems.

articles.title: First-principles description of pumped inelastic x-ray scattering: Example of K-edge RIXS in graphite
articles.abstract: We present an ab initio framework for predicting resonant inelastic x-ray scattering (RIXS) in optically pumped materials. Our methodology is based on the Kramers–Heisenberg formula for the double-differential cross section formulated using the results of the Bethe–Salpeter equation from many-body perturbation theory. To extend this approach to the time domain, we incorporate non-equilibrium charge-carrier distributions obtained from real-time, time-dependent density-functional theory. Generalizing the RIXS implementation with respect to arbitrary polarizations allows us to consider different orientations of incoming and outgoing light. We demonstrate our method’s capabilities by studying RIXS at the K-edge of graphite for various non-equilibrium charge-carrier distributions, representing different delay times after optical pumping. Our results reveal angular dependencies in π - and σ -orbital-derived spectral regions, in good agreement with the experiment.

articles.title: Quantum tunneling on water. III. An asymmetric Marcus-based electron-transfer model for microdroplet redox chemistry
articles.abstract: Water microdroplets support a broad range of spontaneous redox reactions at rates that often exceed expectations from bulk solution, yet a microscopic framework that is both mechanistic and quantitatively predictive across diverse acceptors remains lacking. In Parts I and II [C. Zhuang, N. Qian, and W. Min, J. Chem. Phys. 164 (22), 224709 (2026) and J. Chem. Phys. 164 (22), 224710 (2026)] of this series, we described microdroplet redox chemistry as concerted electron tunneling from partially solvated interfacial hydroxide to acceptors within a symmetric Marcus framework. Here, we extend this picture to an asymmetric, solvation-state-dependent framework in which reactant- and product-side reorganization energies are unequal and evolve along the interfacial dehydration coordinate. This generalization captures the partial breakdown of a single linear-response solvent coordinate at heterogeneous water interfaces and yields a corresponding asymmetric rate expression. Reanalysis of previously studied acceptors confirms consistency with the earlier symmetric model, while revealing that asymmetry becomes decisive in strongly imbalanced cases. Proton reduction by interfacial hydroxide provides a striking example: charge recombination generates highly unequal solvation responses and alters the predicted kinetics by orders of magnitude. Comparison with three independent experimental datasets yields rate estimates in encouraging agreement with experiment, supporting proton reduction as a baseline pathway of intrinsic microdroplet reactivity. A paired comparison of pyridine and benzene further defines a practical boundary for interfacial redox observability. Finally, parity analysis of all acceptors examined across this series shows broad quantitative agreement between predicted and experimentally inferred rate constants. Together, these results establish an asymmetric Marcus framework as a more faithful and predictive theory of electron transfer at heterogeneous water interfaces.

articles.title: Multi-Excitation Front-Face Fluorescence Spectroscopy with Explainable LSTM for Detection of Lymphatic Tissue Adulteration in Ground Beef
articles.title_zh: 多激发正面荧光光谱与可解释的 LSTM 用于检测碎牛肉中的淋巴组织掺假
articles.abstract: Minced beef adulterated with lymphatic tissue presents food-safety, authenticity and economic concerns, optical detection is complicated by variation in fat content, lipid oxidation and muscle type that alter fluorescence independently of adulteration. We therefore combined multi-excitation front-face fluorescence with explainable long short-term memory (LSTM) network to improve specificity. A total of 824 minced beef samples from five commercial slaughterhouses, three breeds, two slaughter-age groups and three muscle cuts, were prepared; 11 spectral outliers were excluded, leaving 813 samples for analysis. Excitation-emission measurements at 280, 322, 340 and 380 nm sampled fluorescence associated with tryptophan, vitamin A, NADH, flavins, collagen cross-links and oxidation. Standard normal variate preprocessing and competitive adaptive reweighted sampling reduced the input variables from 188 to 86 channels, modelled using a shared weight four input LSTM. On the internal test set, model achieved R2P = 0.997, RMSEP = 1.60% w/w and RPD = 19.5. External validation demonstrated performance on two previously unseen slaughterhouses (R2P = 0.988–0.993, RMSEP = 2.60–3.35% w/w, RPD = 9.3–12.0). Interference study (n = 104) incorporating adipose tissue, saline, oxidation and muscle-cut variation, predicted lymphatic content remained below 0.5% w/w and met prespecified equivalence margin of ± 1.0% w/w. SHAP analysis identified increased NADH and reduced tryptophan associated fluorescence as influential predictors. Multi-batch detection limit was 1.8% w/w, whereas reliable quantification began at 6.0% w/w. These results support the use of multi-excitation fluorescence-LSTM analysis for screening lymphatic-tissue adulteration at concentrations relevant to the regulatory thresholds, while reliable quantification near 2% w/w and transferability across instruments remain to established
