articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26449v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum droplets represent a striking manifestation of beyond-mean-field physics, with properties that depend sensitively on dimensionality. Although quantum droplets have been experimentally realized in one and three dimensions, their realization in two dimensions has remained elusive. Here, we observe the formation of a two-dimensional (2D) quantum droplet in a quasi-2D geometry by transferring the single-component Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) into a spin mixture in the Lee-Huang-Yang (LHY) regime, where the LHY effect evidently deviates from its three-dimensional form. We find that, in our scheme, 2D quantum droplets are more stable and exhibit longer lifetimes than previously reported quantum droplets. By instead transferring the initial BECs into another single-spin state with a negative scattering length, we generate 2D Townes solitons. A comparison between the two types of self-bound states shows that, whereas 2D Townes solitons are stable only near a critical atom number determined by the scattering length, 2D quantum droplets remain well-defined and self-bound over a much broader parameter range. These realizations of quantum droplets and Townes solitons in two dimensions provide new insights into self-bound states and open new avenues for exploring nonlinear dynamics in quantum liquids.

articles.title: Exploring ground state phase diagrams of Rydberg atom arrays with finite projected entangled-pair states
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26520v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rydberg atom arrays (RAA) have been advocated as a promising avenue for the quantum simulation of different exotic quantum states. Numerical predictions for the ground state properties of this experimental platform can, however, be challenging in two-dimensional setups. In particular, faithfully treating long-range interactions is often crucial for distinguishing the fate of competing phases, but it usually comes at considerable cost. Projected entangled-pair states (PEPS), optimized via a sampling-based approach, have been shown to deal with such terms on the same ground as shorter-range ones. In this work, we employ these tools to investigate debated physical questions in different frustrated geometries of RAA, from the emergence of spin-glass physics on the Kagomé lattice to topological order beyond the PXP model on the Ruby lattice. By that, we contribute to establishing PEPS as well-suited tools for creating digital twins of RAA experiments.

articles.title: Strain-induced disorder from Schottky gates on high mobility 2DEGs
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26607v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electrostatic gates on two-dimensional electron gases (2DEGs) in GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures are essential for numerous studies of correlation driven phenomena, many performed within the fractional quantum Hall effect. However, the most commonly used type of gates, the metallic Schottky gate, has the propensity to adversely impact the electron mobility and suppress the fractional quantum Hall states. Here we demonstrate through commensurability oscillations under specially designed nanostructured superlattice gates, that strain effects are responsible for the mobility reduction. The experimental results agree well with COMSOL Multiphysics simulations. In a regular, unpatterned gate the disordered, granular nature of the metal film fills the same role as the superlattice in creating a strain field penetrating down to the 2DEG, as we show with a simplified model. These results will help in understanding, improving and finding novel methods to reduce strain-induced disorder in gated high-mobility 2DEGs.

articles.title: Dynamic clustering of active chemotactic Janus particles
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26657v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modeling self-propulsion as an emergent diffusiophoretic effect, we come back to the dynamic clustering experiment of active Janus colloids. Working in the original three-dimensional geometry, and using the chemical solute concentration as a control parameter, we find that the dynamic clustering region occupies a robust fraction of the phase diagram. This behavior is rationalized using a linear stability analysis that efficiently captures the instability of the gas phase to dynamic clusters. We also find that dynamic clustering results from the combined effects of a Keller-Segel collapse and of a motility-induced phase separation, either being arrested by the orientational coupling to the chemical field in agreement with previous work.

articles.title: Vacancy and Helium-Cluster Thermomigration in Tungsten
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26667v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Strong thermal gradients in tungsten plasma-facing components can bias the migration of irradiation-induced defects and thereby alter their redistribution, interaction, and retention. Here, we extend an atomistic jump-statistics framework previously developed for hydrogen to quantify the thermomigration of a single vacancy and interstitial He₁--He₄ clusters in body-centered-cubic tungsten. Non-equilibrium molecular-dynamics simulations performed over several thermal gradients are used to determine the directional jump ratio, while geometrically derived projected jump lengths convert the fitted directional-bias coefficient into the heat-of-transport coefficient Q^*=α kT², where k is the Boltzmann constant, T the temperature, and α a constant. All investigated defects exhibit negative values of α, corresponding to net migration toward the hot region. He₄ has the largest response, α=-2.2457×10⁻² K⁻¹, followed closely by the vacancy, whereas He₃ exhibits the weakest response despite its intermediate cluster size. Independent constant-temperature simulations over 1000--1600 K show that He₃ is also the least mobile cluster and has the largest effective migration energy, Eₘeff=0.271 eV. In contrast, He₄ is more mobile than He₃ and has the smallest effective migration energy, 0.087 eV. Agreement between the He₃ concentration profile predicted from the jump statistics and that obtained from a long molecular-dynamics trajectory provides an independent validation of the method. These results show that thermomigration cannot be inferred from cluster size, diffusivity, or migration energy alone and provide defect-specific heat-of-transport parameters for higher-length-scale models of tungsten under fusion-relevant thermal gradients.

articles.title: Proximity Transient Absorption in van der Waals Heterostructures
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26715v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Transient absorption spectroscopy is a widely used technique for investigating ultrafast electronic dynamics, where transient optical signals are generally interpreted as arising from excitations within the material hosting the probed optical transition. A distinct form of transient absorption spectroscopy, termed proximity transient absorption (PTA), is demonstrated, in which the probed optical transition and the monitored photoexcited carriers reside in different materials. Using graphene/hBN/WS₂ heterostructures, photoexcited carriers in graphene induce a strong transient optical response at the excitonic resonance of a WS₂ monolayer through Coulomb screening, even when the two layers remain electronically isolated by an atomically thin hBN spacer. The resulting signal follows the carrier dynamics of graphene rather than those of WS₂, demonstrating that the WS₂ exciton acts as an optical transducer of electronic processes in a neighboring material. The signal decreases systematically with increasing hBN thickness, confirming its proximity origin while remaining substantial for separations approaching 2 nm. PTA provides a noncontact approach for optically modulating one material using photoexcited carriers in another and enables probing of carrier dynamics in materials that are otherwise difficult to investigate directly. More broadly, PTA establishes a new modality of ultrafast spectroscopy and reveals that transient optical signals in van der Waals heterostructures can originate from excitations residing in spatially separated layers.

articles.title: Collective diffusion of anisotropic hard-particle mixtures
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26721v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Predicting the dynamics of anisotropic mixtures of different species is a challenging theoretical task. We show that Dynamical Density Functional Theory (DDFT), a theory predicting time evolution of the one-particle-density through a free energy functional, can be simplified to a diffusion equation. To quantify the dynamical relaxation behavior, we deduce corrections to the regular long-time collective diffusion coefficients from the direct correlations between the interacting particles and determine these effective diffusion coefficients analytically for a number of hard-particle systems, including mixtures of hard spheres, as well as isotropic and nematic phases of uniaxial spherocylinders and biaxial spherotriangles. Finally, we discuss how to generalize our approach to systems with positional order and suggest a possible application to predicting relaxation times of orientational order parameters.

articles.title: Boundary-Sensitive Quantum Order on Non-Amenable Lattices
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26859v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that quantum systems on non-amenable lattices, whose boundaries constitute an extensive fraction of the system, host novel forms of bulk ordering with no Euclidean counterpart. Combining boundary-retaining iDMRG with an exact symmetry-fixing duality, we investigate p<5 state clock models on the coordination-3 infinite Cayley tree. We find that between the ordered and disordered phases lies an emergent intermediate phase with bulk order induced by an arbitrarily weak boundary field rather than by conventional spontaneous symmetry-breaking. This establishes boundary-sensitive order as a distinct quantum ordering mechanism defying Landau's spontaneous symmetry-breaking paradigm. The intermediate phase realizes a bulk-boundary correspondence in which the unpolarized boundary selects a specific ordered bulk state.

articles.title: Development of microwave multiplexed readout for athermal phonon TES-based detectors
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.24300v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Continued advancements in sub-eV calorimetric measurements are being enabled through the athermal phonon detection channel, with applications spanning a diverse array of fields, including low-mass dark matter searches, coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering, and quantum information science. While Transition Edge Sensors (TESs) have achieved the lowest thresholds to date, they face significant scalability bottlenecks due to the inherent constraints of conventional SQUID readout architectures. To address this limitation, we present an update on R&D to develop practical, highly multiplexed, microwave readout for athermal phonon TESs, which can enable a dramatic increase in both sensor count and target mass, with a focus on sub-GeV dark matter searches as a target application. This work leverages advances from highly scaled mm-wave, x-ray, and gamma-ray TES systems, adapting them to the unique needs of low-threshold rare event measurements. We quantify the basic readout functionality and noise level in our dilution refrigerator testbed and demonstrate operation of a variety of TES devices with saturation powers significantly lower than mm-wave and x-ray devices. We demonstrate proof-of-concept multiplexed readout of background event pulses, bound the readout's contribution to the parasitic TES background load to <1 fW, and discuss a cryogenic inline RF filtering scheme. These results demonstrate practical solutions to several of the key challenges that must be solved before a next-generation athermal phonon detector at scale is realized.

articles.title: CME-SpectrumBench: Can LLMs Analyze Condensed Matter Spectral Data?
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.24304v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are presently well assessed by expert-level mathematics and physics benchmarks which focus on theoretical, symbolic reasoning. However, we lack experimental benchmarks that evaluate data analysis in frontier research problems, a capability that future domain-specific foundation models must have. To this end, we present CME-SpectrumBench, an expert-designed benchmark consisting of 190 questions that measures how reliably frontier LLMs analyze research-level spectral scientific data in condensed matter experiments (CME). Using simulated CME spectral data, we prompt models to identify structures from 2D intensity arrays in the face of noise and limited instrumental resolution, a test of dense context reasoning. Models are scored by how accurately their numerical answers approach the ground truth. Under direct query, scores generally pale in comparison to handwritten code due to clear failure modes: models can find simple features but struggle to trace patterns or compute derived quantities, and performance typically degrades with increased data resolution and noise/convolution levels. LLM performance becomes comparable to handwritten code by allowing tool use (access to a Python interpreter) with/without ReAct prompting, in effect mapping questions onto agentic code generation problems. Our findings show that frontier models can serve as research assistants by interfacing with data through code, but still face difficulties processing information directly from large datasets - a key barrier future foundation models must overcome. The code and data are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/jingene/CMESpectrumBench.

articles.title: Certifying Nonlocal Spin Quantum Entanglement from Local Tunneling Spectra
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.24440v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum entanglement is intrinsically nonlocal, whereas tunneling spectroscopy measures one site at a time. We show that this apparent mismatch can be overcome: local tunneling spectra can certify spin entanglement without coherent control or absolute intensity calibration. An exact spin sum rule turns the high-bias conductance into an internal normalization, allowing the inelastic spin-flip weight to place a lower bound on the local quantum Fisher information. Total-spin conservation then fixes the otherwise inaccessible intersite fluctuation, converting two local spectra into a bound on a collective entanglement witness. We incorporate coupling to the substrate through a spectroscopic bound on spin leakage, while a hierarchy of thresholds distinguishes entanglement between the spins from entanglement with their environment. Including instrumental broadening and noise, the resulting certificate holds at a stated confidence level. These results establish a route for extracting nonlocal quantum information from equilibrium local spectroscopy.

articles.title: Concatenated continuous-drive protection of exchange-based spin-qubit gates
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.24582v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Exchange-based two-qubit gates in semiconductor spin qubits are sensitive to low-frequency detuning noise and control errors. Here, we extend concatenated continuous driving (CCD), implemented by phase modulation of a global microwave drive, to exchange-based SWAP and sqrtSWAP operations between double-dressed spin qubits and investigate its effectiveness for protecting two-qubit gates. We find that CCD retains strong protection against quasistatic common-mode detuning errors while substantially improving robustness against Rabi-frequency errors and qubit-to-qubit Rabi-frequency mismatch compared with conventional continuous dressing. By contrast, the gate fidelity is impacted by differential detuning errors. By modeling partially correlated quasistatic detuning noise, we further show that the noise-averaged gate fidelity depends strongly on the spatial correlation of the qubit-frequency fluctuations, with positive correlations enhancing CCD protection by suppressing the differential-noise component. These results identify the symmetry and spatial correlation of qubit-frequency noise as key factors governing continuous-drive protection in coupled spin-qubit systems.

articles.title: Boosting fluorescence and polarization with nanophotonics for single-molecule chiral sensing
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.24746v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Detecting chirality is essential in chemistry and biomedicine. Circular dichroism identifies chiral molecules through their differential absorption of circularly polarized light. However, its sensitivity is limited by vanishing absorption at low concentrations. Fluorescence-based methods have already enabled other optical techniques to reach the single-molecule limit and could, in principle, also extend chiral detection to reach this sensitivity regime. They are marred, however, by the combination of weak fluorescence signals and low polarization contrast. To overcome these limitations, we leverage high-index dielectric nanophotonics to simultaneously enhance both fluorescence and polarization for chiral sensing. We propose a reciprocity-based analytical framework for a chiral dipolar emitter coupled to a nanoantenna and reveal the different contributions and trade-offs governing the enhancement of circularly polarized fluorescence. Guided by this insight, we tailor achiral dielectric nanostructures to reach a 1000-fold enhancement of fluorescence intensity together with a 10-fold increase in polarization. Crucially, we show that accounting for extrinsic polarization effects in the angular emission patterns of nanophotonic structures is indispensable for reliable enantiomer discrimination. Our approach opens a realistic path for single-molecule chiral sensing.

articles.title: Undulatory Swimming in Sand: Subsurface Locomotion of the Sandfish Lizard
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.24934v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The desert-dwelling sandfish (Scincus scincus) moves within dry sand, a material that displays solid and fluidlike behavior. High-speed x-ray imaging shows that below the surface, the lizard no longer uses limbs for propulsion but generates thrust to overcome drag by propagating an undulatory traveling wave down the body. Although viscous hydrodynamics can predict swimming speed in fluids such as water, an equivalent theory for granular drag is not available. To predict sandfish swimming speed, we developed an empirical model by measuring granular drag force on a small cylinder oriented at different angles relative to the displacement direction and summing these forces over the animal movement profile. The agreement between model and experiment implies that the noninertial swimming occurs in a frictional fluid.

articles.title: Dynamic Hotspot Migration and Self-Induced Resonances in Ultrafast Laser-Irradiated Silicon Thin Films
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.25079v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The spatial distribution of energy in silicon thin films under femtosecond laser irradiation is demonstrated to be influenced by the interaction between carrier-induced refractive index modulation and self-induced Fabry-Pérot resonances. We resolve three characteristic excitation regions such as interface-localized, binodal and multi-nodal regimes considering the analysis of silicon-on-insulator (SOI) configurations across thicknesses of 100, 230, and 350 nm. We report a nonlinear hotspot migration effect where the transient reduction of the refractive index stretches the internal standing wave, translating intensity antinodes toward the film volume during the pulse. Numerical results demonstrate that at higher fluences, plasma-induced extinction suppresses internal reflections, triggering a transition from resonance-mediated absorption to plasma shielding. These findings establish a physical basis for depth-resolved modification in laser nanomanufacturing, providing a dual-capacity for simultaneous surface patterning and depth-resolved subsurface modification with direct applications in laser-assisted interfacial separation and 3D integrated photonic fabrication.

articles.title: Emergent Sparsity: How Many Effective Variables Survive Coarse-Graining in AlphaEarth Embeddings?
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.25258v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AlphaEarth encodes each 10 m land pixel as a 64-component vector intended to support diverse global mapping tasks. Yet many scientific applications work at coarser spatial supports, for which fewer than 64 effective variables may suffice. We ask whether these vectors can be reorganized into ranked global nonlinear coordinates, how many suffice at a chosen reconstruction accuracy, and whether that number decreases with spatial scale. We thus describe effective dimension as a two-control surface over tolerance and spatial scale, rather than one intrinsic number. At each scale, a β-VAE scan with a common architecture produces a rank--distortion envelope, giving the smallest retained count achieved within the scanned family at each reconstruction tolerance. At 3% validation tolerance, this number falls from 24 to 7 when the scale is increased from 10 m to 78.9 km, whereas the corresponding PCA rank falls only from 46 to 38. Repeating the analysis on unit-norm targets preserves this trend.

articles.title: The Anyon Atlas
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.25439v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We classify possible topological quantum field theories in 2+1 dimensions with up to 22 anyons in the bosonic case and up to 26 in the fermionic case, through the modular data of modular and supermodular tensor categories. We construct such data via congruence representations of SL(2,Z) using a numerical optimization algorithm that scales to high rank. We chart the relations between the resulting theories, including anyon condensations and Chern-Simons realizations. We find examples of modular data that do not appear to arise from any Chern-Simons theory by any sequence of condensations of anyons or gaugings of ordinary global symmetries. These examples give qualitatively new topological quantum field theories, which go beyond any notion of gauge theory. For examples in this class with 11 and 12 anyon types, we solve the pentagon and hexagon equations explicitly, showing that these modular data are realized by full unitary topological quantum field theories. We also introduce https://www.AnyonAtlas.org, an online resource for exploring the data.

articles.title: Subsystem quantum Rényi-Bhattacharyya distance in 2D CFTs and its holographic applications
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.25685v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop a systematic method to compute the subsystem fidelity and Rényi fidelity in two-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs) from the operator product expansion of twist operators, and apply it to the subsystem quantum Bhattacharyya distance (BD) and Rényi-Bhattacharyya distance (RBD). We validate the method against exact results in the free massless fermion and boson theories, and then use it to compute the BD and RBD in holographic CFTs between two heavy primary states, between two thermal states, and between a heavy primary state and a thermal state. When the two states differ in their classical, order-c data, the distances are of order c, and the states are distinguishable already at the level of classical gravity; when the leading data coincide, the distances are of order 1/c at every order of the short interval expansion, so that the distinguishability becomes a perturbative quantum gravity effect. For a heavy primary state and its thermal counterpart, the leading contribution to the BD appears at order ell⁸ and is of order c⁰, whereas the RBD is generically of order c, in line with the earlier finding that a heavy primary state and a thermal state share the same order-c entanglement entropy but have different order-c Rényi entropies in the short interval expansion.

articles.title: Phonon-dominated thermal conductivity of a superconducting amorphous MoSi thin film
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26136v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We use the differential 3ω method to directly measure the temperature dependent thermal conductivity for about 90 nm Mo0.78Si0.22 thin films. The measurements are performed in a closed-cycle cryostat to access the temperature range between 50 K and 300 K. The MoSi thin films are capped with Al2O3 and probed with a Pt wire. The results show that the thermal conductivity does not satisfy the Wiedemann-Franz law. This implies that thermal transport in MoSi is not dominated by electrons but by phonon-like excitations, contrary to what is assumed in many electro-thermal models of superconducting devices. We argue that this property might be related to the weak localization visible in the resistivity as a function of temperature curves of the superconductor.

articles.title: Universal Quantum Criticality from a Gaussian Variational Manifold
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26246v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Universal behavior at continuous phase transitions is encoded in long-wavelength fixed-point theories controlled by dimensionality and symmetries. It is a central question for which systems this universal behavior and the underlying long-wavelength description can be captured by a noninteracting theory allowing for analytical and accurate predictions. In this work we provide a systematic procedure for obtaining the best noninteracting fermionic description of a quantum phase transition through fermionic Gaussian states. We demonstrate the performance of our procedure for the interacting long-range transverse-field Ising chain. This formulation reduces the problem to a self-consistent Euler equation that yields a critical line in close agreement with independent numerical benchmarks, while its singular momentum structure provides analytic predictions for continuously varying critical properties. Yet exact diagonalization shows that Gaussian-state fidelity to the exact ground state is poorest, and non-Gaussianity strongest, near the transition. Thus, accurate predictions for critical properties can emerge from the Gaussian variational description even where its microscopic wave-function approximation is weakest.

articles.title: End-to-End Optimization of Partial Fault Tolerance in Neutral-Atom Arrays
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26471v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fault-tolerant (FT) quantum computation offers a pathway to quantum advantage, but its realization is hindered by its significant overhead. The partially FT "STAR" architecture reduces the cost of universal computation at the price of relaxing FT requirements for non-Clifford operations, increasing exposure to hardware noise. Therefore, maximizing its performance and applicability demands careful co-design with the underlying hardware. In this work we investigate the co-design of the STAR architecture with neutral-atom platforms, connecting the underlying atomic physics to logical error modeling and application-level performance. At the physical level, we identify a favorable noise bias in ¹⁷¹Yb Rydberg gates, and show how it can be enhanced through error-selective pulse optimization. At the logical level, we identify an intrinsic error suppression mechanism, yielding vanishing logical coherent noise in leading order. Detailed circuit-level simulations of surface code implementations show more than an order of magnitude reduction in logical error relative to previous estimates. As a concrete target application, we focus on the Fermi-Hubbard model with periodic boundaries, for which we design a simulation circuit particularly suited to early implementations. We quantify the resource tradeoff of partially and fully FT approaches to gate synthesis, with the former showing approximately an order of magnitude reduction in state-injection depth, and an even larger reduction in Clifford resources. Comparing with classical and fully FT approaches, we identify regimes where partial fault tolerance provides both lower overheads and lower error rates. In our estimates, this is accessible with moderate error rates psim 10⁻³ and a few thousand qubits, underlining that for these types of problems, partial FT approaches provide a compelling pathway to early quantum advantage.

articles.title: Non-Markovian exceptional points and information backflow: a Heisenberg reaction-coordinate approach
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26620v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The primary pathway to the investigation of exceptional points (EPs) in open quantum systems has been the use of Markovian master equations. However, recently it has been realised that they can arise in settings that show non-Markovian behaviour. The main approach in this direction has been the use of pseudomodes, which allow the influence of a structured environment to be replaced by new damped auxiliary modes. In this work, we use a Heisenberg-equation approach which relies on the reaction-coordinate formalism to obtain exact analytical dynamics. First, we show how our method considerably simplifies the analysis compared to the use of master equations. Second, we utilise it to discuss non-Markovian revivals in systems with second and higher-order EPs, showing that the notion that EPs demarcate the onset of revivals is not generally true. We then utilise our results to discuss the dynamical effects of higher-order non-Markovian EPs, deriving bounds on the number of revivals and investigating enhanced asymptotic relaxation near higher-order EPs. Finally, we investigate non-Markovian EPs with engineered reservoirs and show how they can be utilised to control the rate of irreversible information loss.

articles.title: Physics-Constrained Modeling and Inference of the Equation of State for Dissociative Materials
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26791v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Equations of state (EOSs) describe how a material's internal energy and pressure change with temperature and density. They are inputs to hydrodynamic simulations in materials science and planetary science. We model the ion-thermal free-energy term for dissociative materials, where molecular bonds break apart to form new species under extreme conditions. This term is governed by two latent physical processes, a molar-mass surface and a Debye-temperature curve, neither of which is observed directly. Instead, both must be recovered from internal energy and pressure, which are derivatives of the free energy, subject to thermodynamic constraints. Existing EOS tables are typically built through material-specific hand-tuning, a process that is tedious, does not scale across materials or conditions, and offers no guarantee of thermodynamic consistency. We propose a partitioned statistical framework that infers molar mass and Debye temperature directly from EOS data, guaranteeing thermodynamic consistency by construction. Local molar-mass behavior is captured with polynomial basis functions across domain partitions, while the Debye temperature is modeled with an I-spline basis. In simulations and a carbon dioxide case study, the method accurately recovers the underlying physical quantities, improves prediction of held-out energy and pressure data, and provides uncertainty quantification while scaling with EOS table size.

articles.title: Field theory guides Monte Carlo in the one-dimensional long-range Ising model
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26838v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The statistical long-range Ising (LRI) model in one dimension provides a family of some of the simplest non-exactly solvable critical points. These critical points are described by long-range conformal field theories (CFTs) that are well understood analytically with perturbative expansions and some exact results. Guided by this, we revisit the Monte Carlo (MC) approach to the corresponding lattice model which has many favorable features compared to other systems studied with MC methods. In particular, with very modest computational cost, we are able to estimate scaling dimensions of leading and subleading operators as well as the associated three-point functions, and even certain four-point functions. These results help highlight the fact that 1d LRI CFTs are a phenomenal playground to more generally test non-perturbative methods and ideas for strongly coupled CFTs.

articles.title: Absorbing state transitions with long-range annihilation
articles.abstract: arXiv:2409.03280v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a family of classical stochastic processes describing diffusive particles undergoing branching and long-range annihilation in the presence of a parity constraint. The probability for a pair-annihilation event decays as a power-law in the distance between particles, with a tunable exponent. Such long-range processes arise naturally in various classical settings, and increasingly play a role in the study of quantum dynamics: for example, quantum state preparation or error correction processes aim to prepare ordered ground states, which requires removing point-like excitations in pairs via non-local feedback operations conditioned on a global set of measurement outcomes. We analytically and numerically describe features of absorbing phases and phase transitions in this family of classical models as pairwise annihilation is performed at larger and larger distances. Notably, we find that the two canonical absorbing-state universality classes -- directed-percolation and parity-conserving -- are endpoints of a new line of universality classes with continuously varying critical exponents. These new classes follow from an interplay of long-range interactions and symmetries: decreasing the long-range exponent effectively weakens the local effects of global symmetry constraints. This competition significantly broadens known non-equilibrium phases and phase transitions.

articles.title: Coherence and pairing enhancement in a trilayer cuprate with layer-selective charge order
articles.abstract: arXiv:2506.01448v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Trilayer cuprates hold the record for the highest superconducting critical temperatures (Tc), yet the underlying mechanism remains elusive. Using time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (tr-ARPES), we uncover a striking interplay between charge order, superconducting gap magnitude, and quasiparticle coherence in Bi₂Sr₂Ca₂Cu₃O₁₀₊δ (Bi2223). We present ARPES-based evidence of charge order on the inner CuO₂ plane -- as confirmed via resonant x-ray scattering (RXS) -- and show that the same inner plane hosts a large superconducting gap matching its doping, firmly establishing it as underdoped. Despite its underdoped nature, the inner plane also exhibits an exceptional degree of quasiparticle coherence; suppressing charge-order fluctuations further enhances this, making it comparable to that of the overdoped outer planes at elevated electronic temperatures. At the same time, on the overdoped outer planes we find larger superconducting gaps than what is seen on comparably doped single and bilayer cuprates, indicating an unexpected and simultaneous enhancement of both coherence and pairing interactions in Bi2223. These findings, supported by complementary single- and three-layer Hubbard model calculations, reveal a unique interlayer mechanism in which both pairing strength and phase coherence are optimized when interfacing planes with distinct hole concentrations, providing new microscopic insight into the record Tc of Bi2223.

articles.title: Quantum Geometric Injection and Shift Optical Forces Drive Coherent Phonons
articles.abstract: arXiv:2507.17814v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a gauge-invariant quantum-geometric theory of light-induced Raman forces driving coherent lattice dynamics in solids. We show that the resonant interband response separates into injection and shift forces, providing the lattice analogue of injection and shift photocurrents. Crucially, the electronic quantum metric and Berry curvature directly govern these forces, weighted by distinct electron--phonon quantities. The injection force is controlled by the quantum geometric tensor and differences between band-diagonal electron--phonon couplings, producing the resonant displacive response. The shift force is a resonant impulsive response governed by quantum geometry and a phononic shift vector arising from interband electron--phonon coherence. We derive polarization selection rules, symmetry constraints, and temporal signatures. Applied to interlayer shear phonons in a bilayer Haldane model, the theory predicts tunability with optical frequency, topology, electronic temperature, and current-induced symmetry breaking. These results establish a quantum-geometric framework for coherent lattice dynamics and identify coherent phonons as experimentally accessible signatures of electronic quantum geometry in quantum materials.

articles.title: Kolmogorov-type non-thermal fixed points and beyond of far-from-equilibrium dilute system: ultra-cold Fermi gas
articles.abstract: arXiv:2508.18821v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The far-from-equilibrium dynamics driven by the scattering from next-to-leading-order (NLO) corrections in the quantum field theory has stationary solutions for the particle distribution characterized as the Kolmogorov-type non-thermal fixed points corresponding to scale-invariant particle/energy flux. The dynamics of the spatially homogeneous dilute ultra-cold Fermi gas is investigated, and its kinetic equation confirms the Kolmogorov-type non-thermal fixed points in the perturbation theory by the quasi-particle assumption, in contrast to the wave turbulence of the ultra-cold Bose gas. In addition, other stationary states are discussed when the the vertex correction becomes significant in the kinetic equation. It is found that conditions for the scale-invariant flux in this case no longer hold when the quasi-particle assumption is applied.

articles.title: Casimir-Polder energy landscape: Unipolarizable atom and ring
articles.abstract: arXiv:2602.20203v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Casimir-Polder interaction energy between a unipolarizable point atom and a unipolarizable dielectric ring has been limited, until now, to the case when the atom is confined on the axis of symmetry of the ring. We find the generalized analytical expression for any position of the atom relative to the ring in terms of complete elliptic integrals. This is aided by the construction of a class of integrals of a Jacobian elliptic function as a linear combination of complete elliptic integrals. Our expression for the interaction energy allows us to investigate the instability of the atom even for the equilibrium points which exists off the axis of symmetry.

articles.title: Interaction and disorder effects on Cooper instability in two-dimensional fractional Dirac semimetals
articles.abstract: arXiv:2602.22772v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Employing a renormalization group analysis that allows for an unbiased treatment of competing physical ingredients, we systematically trace how the interplay between Cooper pairing and disorder scatterings governs the emergence or suppression of Cooper instability in the low-energy regime of fractional Dirac semimetals.In the clean limit, we find that the emergence of Cooper instability requires surpassing a finite interaction threshold |λ_c|, and depends sensitively on both the fractional exponent α and the transfer momentum Q=(Q,φ). Specifically, bigger values of α enhance the tendency toward BCS instability. For αin(0.001,0.61), the (Q,φ) parameter space separates into two distinct regions: Zone-uppercaseexpandafterromannumeral1, where Cooper instability is suppressed, and Zone-uppercaseexpandafterromannumeral2, where it is allowed. In the presence of disorders, we demonstrate that they can either promote or suppress Cooper instability. Disorder of type Δ₁ or Δ₂ enhances superconductivity by reducing the critical interaction threshold |λ_c| and expanding the superconducting phase space (Zone-uppercaseexpandafterromannumeral2). In sharp contrast, either Δ₀ or Δ₃ suppresses Cooper pairing by increasing |λ_c| and shrinking the available phase space (Zone-uppercaseexpandafterromannumeral1). Although Cooper instability can be enhanced when promotive disorders (Δ₁, Δ₂) coexist with a single suppressive disorder (Δ₀ or Δ₃), the suppressive influence of Δ₀,₃ generally dominates the promotive effects of Δ₁,₂ in the presence of all sorts of disorders. These results would be helpful for further studies of fractional Dirac semimetals and alike materials.

articles.title: Horizon-Boundary Localization of the Hawking Temperature in a Weak AdS/CFT Extension
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.23916v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a conditional boundary-localization statement for the Hawking temperature. For a static, Euclideanizable black hole with a non-degenerate horizon, the temperature is determined entirely by the first non-vanishing near-horizon data. This result is obtained consistently through three approaches: removal of the Euclidean conical defect, the horizon boundary term in the two-dimensional Gauss-Bonnet theorem, and a complex residue calculation. In asymptotically anti-de Sitter spacetime, the Euclidean time periodicity selected at the horizon extends to the conformal boundary, so the boundary conformal field theory inherits the same thermal period up to time normalization. This provides only a weak, temperature-sector extension of the AdS/CFT framework and does not imply a full duality. For dynamical spherical spacetimes, the Hamilton-Jacobi analysis selects the trapping or apparent horizon as the local thermal boundary, whereas a separated event horizon is generally not associated with the relevant pole. Vaidya and charged-Vaidya examples support this boundary-selection picture and reduce to the standard stationary result when the horizons coincide. The construction is further checked using anti-de Sitter black holes, numerical contour calculations, limiting cases, and an extremal counterexample. The result concerns where the Hawking temperature is localized and does not replace the quantum-field-theoretic mechanism of Hawking radiation.

articles.title: Finite quantum gravity in locally conformally flat spacetime through covariant spectral regularization
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.23924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pure gravity quantum gravity (pure gravity QG) is non-renormalizable at two and higher loop level. One of the main characteristics of objects occurring in QG is their Lorentz covariance. QG necessitates the analysis of a collection of Lorentz covariant terms of higher and higher order, which is not feasible using renormailization. This paper describes how the regularization technique known as covariant spectral regularization (CSR) can be used to analyze Lorentz covariant 4-tensor valued measures on Minkowski space. The graviton vacuum polarization tensor is cast as such a measure and CSR is used to obtain a well defined and finite function representing this tensor. This is then used to compute the Feynman amplitudes for examples of one-loop, two-loop and n-loop graviton-graviton scattering in pure gravity QG. The CSR method results in functions (densities) representing divergent Feynman integrals without requiring renormalization or counterterms. Therefore it can be used to analyze arbitrarily complicated multiloop QG Feynman diagrams without being crippled by a proliferation of counterterms, as is classical QG.

articles.title: Two Cosmological Histories in a New Exponential Infrared f(T) Teleparallel Gravity: Implications for the Hubble Tension and the Low-ell Planck TT--EE Tension
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.23956v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate a particular case of the New Exponential Infrared f(T) teleparallel gravity model with the same number of free parameters as the standard ΛCDM model. Remarkably, due to the two real branches of the Lambert function W, the model admits two distinct cosmological solutions, denoted by f⁽I⁾CDM and f⁽II⁾CDM. The former exhibits a late-time phantom crossing, whereas the latter predicts an effective dark-energy density evolving from negative to positive values. Using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo analysis of the Planck CMB, DESI BAO, and Type Ia supernova data, we find that the f⁽II⁾CDM branch develops a bimodal posterior distribution in the primordial parameters Aₛ and τ ᵣₑᵢₒ for the Planck-only dataset. We show that this bimodality originates from the tension between the low-ell TT and EE likelihoods, which becomes pronounced in models exhibiting a significantly enhanced late ISW contribution relative to the ΛCDM model. Moreover, the inclusion of background observations drives this branch toward cosmologically unacceptable parameter values, rendering it observationally unviable. The f⁽I⁾CDM branch, on the other hand, remains observationally viable, yielding H₀=73.43±0.69~mathrmkm,s⁻¹,Mpc⁻¹ for the Planck-only dataset and H₀=72.55±0.32~mathrmkm,s⁻¹,Mpc⁻¹ after including DESI, substantially alleviating the Hubble tension. Although this branch provides a slightly better fit than ΛCDM for Planck-only data, the addition of background observations reverses this preference in favor of the standard ΛCDM model. These results show that the cosmological viability of this model critically depends on the choice of the Lambert W branch, with only the f⁽I⁾CDM solution remaining compatible with current cosmological observations.

articles.title: Transient Heat Conduction on Quantum Hardware: Replicated Temperature-Field Reconstruction and Shot-Count Sensitivity with a Variational Quantum Linear Solver
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.24004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Implicit discretizations of transient heat conduction repeatedly generate sparse linear systems, making diffusion problems a natural test bed for quantum linear solvers. This study evaluates how accurately a variational quantum linear solver (VQLS) recovers the temperature field produced by one backward-Euler step of one-dimensional conduction on IBM quantum hardware. A pre-specified confirmatory experiment compares N=4 interior temperatures encoded on two qubits with N=8 temperatures encoded on three qubits using ten paired hardware blocks; a separately defined N=16, four-qubit extension is evaluated in five independently scheduled exploratory blocks. Local VQLS optimization reduces relative temperature-field error to approximately 10⁻⁸ for all three cases, establishing an essentially exact ideal reference at this scale. On hardware, mean relative L2 temperature-field error is 8.07% for N=4 and 20.14% for N=8, a paired increase of 12.06 percentage points (95% CI, 10.71-13.42; exact paired sign-flip p=0.001953). The exploratory N=16 mean is 24.75+/-1.84%. A pre-specified N=16 shot-count follow-up then evaluates the same locked circuit at 2,048, 8,192, and 32,768 shots in six independently scheduled blocks. Mean field error remains 23.64%, 24.57%, and 24.37%, respectively; the 32,768-minus-2,048-shot contrast is +0.74 percentage points (95% CI, -0.65 to 2.12; p=0.281). In contrast, ideal multinomial sampling predicts a reduction from 2.68% to 0.75%. Higher shot counts reduce block-to-block variability but do not recover the mean cold-side temperature field. The results show that full-field readout of a strongly nonuniform thermal state is limited by more than ordinary finite-shot sampling under the tested hardware conditions, motivating observable-focused quantum formulations for heat flux, stored energy, and selected temperatures.

articles.title: Revealing Detailed Transport Mechanisms in Silicon Tunneling Diodes
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.24088v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding carrier transport in heavily doped semiconductor junctions is essential for developing next-generation tunneling devices for cryogenic electronics and steep-slope technologies. In this work, we investigate the transport mechanisms in a silicon tunneling diode using extensive TCAD (Technology Computer Aided Design) simulations benchmarked against electrical measurements over a wide temperature range of 4 K to 440 K. The measured device characteristics show no negative differential conductance, strong temperature dependence of forward current with a nearly constant semi-logarithmic slope, and weak temperature dependence under high reverse bias. To identify the mechanisms underlying these characteristics, we investigate the contributions of band-to-band tunneling (BTBT), trap-assisted tunneling (TAT), Shockley-Read-Hall (SRH) recombination, and avalanche generation. We also enhance the Schenk TAT model by incorporating Fermi-Dirac statistics to accurately capture the transport behavior at lower temperatures. Under forward bias, TAT in the depletion region dominates the current at low-to-moderate voltages, whereas SRH becomes increasingly significant at higher voltages and temperatures. Under reverse bias, TAT dominates at low reverse voltages, particularly near and above room temperatures, whereas BTBT becomes predominant at high reverse bias, resulting in weak temperature dependence. This work provides a comprehensive understanding of the bias- and temperature-dependent transport mechanisms in silicon tunneling junctions and an enhanced TAT model suitable over a broader range of operating conditions.

articles.title: A consistent coupled level-set and volume-of-fluid solver for two-phase flow in OpenFOAM
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.24225v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coupled level-set and volume-of-fluid methods combine the mass conservation of a transported volume fraction with the smooth interface description of a signed-distance function. In the simple coupled variant, the level set is rebuilt from the volume fraction during every time step rather than transported, and it supplies the interface curvature and the fluid properties. This paper presents an implementation of the simple coupled method in OpenFOAM and sets out four conditions that such an implementation must satisfy to stay consistent. The density in the time derivative and in the convective mass flux of the momentum equation must be the same field, the curvature in the surface tension force must come from the level set, the blended kinematic viscosity must reproduce the blended dynamic viscosity, and the smoothed fields must be evaluated on boundary and processor patches as well as in the cells. The solver is tested on the second two-dimensional rising-bubble case of Hysing et al. on two meshes. Up to t= 1.75 s, while the three reference codes of that benchmark agree, the rise velocity differs from the reference by at most 0.0064 and 0.0073 m/s on the two meshes, and its first maximum is 1.3% and 2.0% below the reference. These differences grow slightly with refinement. The same happens when the curvature and the properties are taken from the volume fraction, which reproduces the standard OpenFOAM solver, so their cause lies outside the coupling. Over the same interval the level-set coupling stays closer to the reference than this volume-fraction coupling, with a largest velocity difference of 0.0073 against 0.0094 m/s on the finer mesh. The bubble volume is conserved to the printed precision, and a run on four processors matches the serial run. The solver is released under the GNU General Public License.

articles.title: Microcomb spectral fingerprinting enables parts-per-trillion methane detection with low humidity cross-sensitivity
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.24338v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical frequency combs have transformed molecular spectroscopy by enabling broadband, high-resolution analysis, yet they are conventionally used as light sources to interrogate external samples. Here, we introduce an integrated microcomb sensing architecture that unifies resonantly enhanced evanescent sensing with multiwavelength molecular fingerprinting in a single ultrahigh-quality-factor silica microresonator. Gaseous analytes interact directly with the evanescent field of light recirculating within the resonator, enhancing sensitivity while encoding analyte-induced perturbations across the microcomb's collective spectral response. Rather than relying on a single optical resonance, we exploit distributed responses across multiple comb lines to generate multidimensional molecular fingerprints. Adding more comb lines systematically improves analyte discrimination, showing that the microcomb provides sensing information beyond what individual spectral channels offer. Using methane as a model analyte, we achieve an estimated detection limit of 178 parts per trillion, with minimal spectral responses to ammonia, carbon monoxide, hexane, and water vapor at relative humidities up to 90%. By replacing physically long interaction paths with resonant light recirculation in an ultrahigh-Q microresonator, this architecture brings compact optical sensing into the parts-per-trillion regime while exploiting distributed spectral information for chemical identification.

articles.title: Freeform gradient-index media reconstruction
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.24393v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reconstructing a gradient-index (GRIN) medium consists of determining a spatial refractive index distribution that produces a prescribed ray trajectory, an inverse problem in geometrical optics. Previous approaches have used geometrical symmetries and conserved ray quantities to address this inverse problem. Extending reconstruction to freeform media requires approaches that do not rely on these symmetries. Here, we present a three-dimensional point-wise method for reconstructing freeform GRIN media through the inverse application of local refraction. The method does not require geometrical symmetry, paraxial approximations, or prior knowledge of the iso-indicial surfaces, and is straightforward to implement. Reconstruction using two interface geometries demonstrates that different refractive index distributions can be obtained from the same prescribed trajectory function. The choice of interfaces thus provides an additional degree of freedom for optical design, subject to local refraction conditions and compatibility between overlapping reconstructed regions.

articles.title: SIESTA-QCOMP: Bridging Classical and Quantum Computing for Strongly Correlated Systems
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.24616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Density Functional Theory (DFT) is the established workhorse of computational materials science, yet it faces fundamental challenges with strongly correlated electrons, such as in transition metal complexes and bond-breaking processes. While quantum computing offers a theoretically exact path to resolve these problems, current hardware limitations prohibit fully quantum simulations of realistic material systems. To bridge this gap, we present SIESTA-QCOMP, a modular suite embedding quantum methodologies within DFT. Harnessing SIESTA's localised basis set, we implement a projection-based embedding scheme that treats the bulk environment classically while mapping the strongly correlated "impurity" subspace to a quantum processor. The architecture uses a socket-based driver to orchestrate workflows between the Fortran-based SIESTA engine and Python-based frameworks like Qiskit, ensuring high interoperability. We detail the hybrid workflow, currently utilising a Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE), and discuss the road map toward methods such as Sample-based Quantum Diagonalisation (SQD). We illustrate the framework on an hypothetical iron porphyrin calculation and argue that such hybrid architectures are not merely interim solutions but essential foundations for integrating quantum utility into materials design, as envisioned by our broader QCOMP4DFT initiative.

articles.title: Rovibrational dynamics in strongly-coupled gas-phase methane
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.24654v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Polaritons, the hybrid light-matter states formed when molecular transitions are strongly coupled to an optical cavity mode, appear to alter chemical dynamics, reactivity, and photophysics, though the mechanisms and reproducibility of these effects remain hotly debated. Nearly all reports in polariton chemistry rest on spectroscopic measurements of optical cavity transmission. Interpretation of these experiments therefore relies on understanding the linear and nonlinear spectroscopy of strongly-coupled systems. Working in the gas phase can dramatically simplify spectroscopic observables, as the intermolecular and environmental interactions that complicate the response of condensed-phase systems can be minimized. Our prior work introduced a platform for gas-phase molecular polaritons and demonstrated that linear cavity transmission spectra in the strong coupling regime are well described with classical Fabry-Pérot cavity physics. Here, we extend this platform to the nonlinear spectroscopy of cavity-coupled rovibrational transitions of methane. We monitor transient changes in the cavity transmission spectrum following optical pumping of intracavity molecules via an axis orthogonal to the longitudinal cavity axis. We find that the classical Fabry-Pérot cavity treatment quantitatively reproduces our transient spectra and allows for extraction of the collisional relaxation and transport timescales of intracavity molecules. We observe no difference in the dynamics of strongly-coupled methane versus free-space, non-cavity control experiments. This effort connects our gas-phase work to the much larger body of transient condensed-phase polariton spectroscopy and represents a step towards predictive understanding of molecular dynamics under strong coupling.

articles.title: Second-Order Correction for Statistical Bias in Monte Carlo Depletion Calculations
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.24932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Depletion analyses are often driven by Monte Carlo neutron transport methods that introduce uncertainty into the transmutation matrix used to evolve a material composition. The nonlinearity of the matrix exponential applied to this transmutation matrix causes the uncertainty to introduce a systematic bias in the computed isotope vectors. This work derives a second-order correction for this bias that can be computed with quantities obtainable from typical Monte Carlo transport routines. An augmented Bateman system is formulated to evaluate these quantities and an adapted Chebyshev rational approximation method uses transmutation matrix factorizations for efficient evaluation of the second-order correction. Then, the correction is demonstrated using a ten-nuclide verification problem, an ITER port-plug activation problem, and a 9-pin boiling water reactor lattice containing self-shielded gadolinium-bearing fuel.

articles.title: Superradiant temporal transition radiation of a relativistic electron beam
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.25165v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A charge in uniform motion carries a bound field that does not radiate. Transition radiation releases part of it at a boundary in space. We propose and analyze the case of radiation emission due to a boundary in time: a relativistic electron bunch passes through an aperture in a semiconductor (silicon) wafer, and while its bound field occupies the wafer, a femtosecond laser switches the semiconductor into an electron-hole plasma. The field is a valid solution of the old medium and not of the new one, so it is handed to the plasma as an initial condition for radiation emission at the plasma frequency. Because in temporal transition radiation (t-TR) the wavevector is conserved, and the frequency is not, the emission can appear in a spectral band that the bunch's own field does not populate. Every electron contributes in phase to the initial condition at the switching moment, so the emitted energy scales as N². We derive the field energy conversion at the temporal boundary and the resultant measurable amplitude and frequency line-shape of the radiation taking into consideration plasma carriers collisional loss. The simplified analytical model of the process and its scaling laws are confirmed by use of FDTD numerical computations for a reference case based on the parameters of an existing 6.5 MeV photoinjector accelerator. For this case we predict wideband t-TR radiation emission at THz frequencies, where the emission center frequency, near the plasma frequency, is selectable across an octave, set by the laser fluence, and the intensity is governed by the beam charge. The predicted radiative energy is detectable in a single shot. The experimental considerations for observing it are given in a Supplement.

articles.title: Multigroup Implicit Monte Carlo Radiation Hydrodynamics on Moving Voronoi Meshes with STORM and RICH
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.25174v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present and validate an Implicit Monte Carlo (IMC) radiation-transport solver in the open-source, mesh-agnostic storm library, coupled to the moving-mesh hydrodynamics code rich in three-dimensional Voronoi tessellations. The solver is multigroup, or continuous in frequency, throughout; it transforms photon packets exactly between the comoving and laboratory frames, books every exchange with the material as a laboratory four-momentum so that the IMC path conserves energy to roundoff, formulates the Fleck factor in the fluid's proper time, and accelerates optically thick cells with multigroup Discrete Diffusion Monte Carlo (DDMC) behind an emissivity-preserving interface. We tested the solver on a broad suite of benchmark problems, and it performed well on all of them. The solver is built on the MPI-parallel Monte Carlo framework of storm, which scales to 13,440 cores.

articles.title: One Component Plasmas Frequency Moments from the ISF
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.25209v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamic structural characteristics of classical one component plasmas (OCP) are an essential tool for understanding of strongly coupled plasmas through experiments and numerical simulations. Here, instead of the dynamic structure factor, we focus our attention on the intermediate scattering function (ISF). Theoretical results are compared to those of obtained by the method of molecular dynamics (MD).

articles.title: Negative partisanship drives anti-frontrunner volatility in election dynamics
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.25210v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Negative partisanship---where voter mobilization is driven primarily by aversion toward an opposing candidate rather than positive alignment---profoundly reshapes modern electoral dynamics. Here, we formulate a two-dimensional piecewise map to model campaign opinion dynamics, where voter abstention arises endogenously from a latent spectrum of voter activation barriers. We show that cross-candidate rejection sensitivity triggers a non-smooth collapse of abstention, dividing the phase space into an under-mobilized regime and a fully mobilized campaign regime. In symmetric elections with radicalized voter bases, spontaneous symmetry breaking via a pitchfork bifurcation gives rise to asymmetric polling attractors partitioned by mirror-symmetric basins of attraction, where early public perceptions---encoded in initial campaign conditions---act as a deterministic catalyst selecting candidate lead lock-in long before election day. For elevated cross-rejection, the symmetric equilibrium destabilizes via a period-doubling flip bifurcation, driving persistent anti-frontrunner polling swings. Rather than predicting static candidate hegemony, our model reveals that high negative partisanship turns elections into time-sensitive dynamical systems, where final election outcomes reflect discrete sampling snapshots of an oscillating campaign trajectory.

articles.title: Reduced Molecular Plasma Kinetics with Non-Boltzmann Vibrational Distribution
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.25738v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vibrational kinetics can strongly affect energy transfer, chemical kinetics, and discharge behavior in molecular plasmas, but resolving all internal states is often impractical for reactor-scale simulation. Compact, physics-based vibrational closures are particularly needed when complete state-to-state (StS) data are limited. Starting from a detailed H₂ StS plasma-kinetics framework coupled to an electron-Boltzmann calculation, this work develops a reduced vibrational-kinetics formulation. The H₂ vibrational ladder is reduced to two non-Boltzmann groups that evolve their population and internal energy. State-resolved reaction rates and associated energy-exchange terms are projected onto the groups for subsequent tabulation in reactor-scale plasma models. StS-informed samples of the reduced-model are propagated for pulsed RF H₂ plasmas across a scan of pulse-averaged absorbed power and compared with the corresponding StS simulations. Predictions from the sampled models reproduce the bulk plasma response, including electron density, atomic-H density, and H₃⁺ density. Discrepancies in H⁻ production and the upper-energy-group vibrational temperature persist across the sampled reductions. This indicates a limitation of the present VDF reconstruction rather than the nominal parameter choice. Tail-sensitive processes therefore require a more accurate representation of the vibrational distribution.

articles.title: Decoherence of the pair entangled states at thermalization and interparticle interaction. Heisenberg--Wigner path integral Monte Carlo simulations
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26033v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For deeper understanding of quantum non-local correlations a new path integral real-time quantum dynamics approach has been developed and applied to the Monte Carlo simulation of the decoherence of pair entangled states in many-body systems in the framework of the ``replica trick''. Calculations have been carried out for the Heisenberg-Wigner path integral representation of the entangled state correlation function (ESCF) in the modified unified electron gas model as example. The Wiener-Khinchin transformation of ESCF has been applied to random paths in path integral allowing for the Monte Carlo simulation of ESCF. Presented results include the spin-resolved radial distribution functions, ESCFs and estimations of the decoherence time of the entangled electron pairs due to thermalization and interparticle interaction.

articles.title: Experimental verification of the PRIORA Monte Carlo code for proton radiography
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26121v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: PRIORA (Proton Radiography Ion-Optical Ray-tracing Analysis) is a fast Monte Carlo model for high-energy proton radiography. It combines fitted proton-matter interaction tables with energy-dependent transfer maps of arbitrary order and simulates approximately 10⁶ protons/s through a complete ion-optical system on an 8-core laptop. We verify it with GSI data obtained with the Ta_bench target: fifteen precision slits in a 2 mm Ta plate between symmetric PMMA staircases. A single experimental image provides the image scale, spatial resolution as a function of chromatic load, signed focus in both planes, effective angular acceptance and multiple-scattering contrast. With identical processing of experiment and simulation and no physics adjustment, PRIORA reproduces the data obtained with 2 and 4 GeV protons. At 2 GeV, PRIORA also recovers sub-percent quadrupole trims consistent with the control-system records and determines a target-plane spatial resolution of 115±6,μm.

articles.title: Demonstration of continuous non-invasive monitoring of plant metabolism using mid-infrared photoacoustic spectroscopy
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26172v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Life is a rhythmic process driven by cellular and physiological mechanisms that allow plants to respond and adapt to their environment. In addition to natural fluctuations, plants are increasingly exposed to environmental stresses, mainly caused by climate change and anthropogenic pollution. Multiple approaches across different biological scales (gene, cell, metabolite, and physiology) have shed light on acclimation mechanisms but generally lack sufficient temporal resolution. Establishing a non-invasive and high-temporal-resolution monitoring method to measure plant activity across different conditions is therefore needed to fully assess how plant metabolism changes under stress. Here, we established a novel approach to perform continuous and non-invasive mid-infrared photoacoustic spectroscopy on vascular plants, with the aim of identifying and monitoring the chemical composition of peripheral tissues, including sap, over periods ranging from a few minutes to several months. We describe an experimental setup, the physics underlying its operation, and present a multi-day acquisition. Compared with controls, data enabled to identify a diurnal pattern, with peaks of approximately equal duration, that recurred consistently over the experiment. Estimations of the impact of instrumental and environmental fluctuations indicate that the signal amplitude and trends cannot be explained by instrumental drifts. The experiment thus demonstrated the detection of a signal associated with plant physiological activity. While its origins remain to be clarified, this preliminary experiment demonstrates the feasibility of the measurements and provides a basis for future developments.

articles.title: Vibro-acoustic optimisation of sandwich panels using the wave/finite element method
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26192v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates the use of a wave-based method in the framework of structural optimisation of composite panels involving advanced components. The wave/finite element method (WFEM) is used to evaluate the influence of a core's geometry on the transition frequency of a sandwich panel involving composite skins. This transition occurs is a sandwich panel when the transverse shear stiffness has a significant influence on the flexural motion, compared to the bending stiffness. It follows that the modal density and the acoustic radiation will considerably increase above this frequency. The periodic waveguide is modelled at the mesoscopic scale using a 3D finite element model of the unit-cell. Therefore this method does not require an homogenisation of the core based on Gibson and Ashby formulations to provide the wave dispersion characteristics. Although the cellular cores compared in this study share the same mass-to-stiffness ratio, a significant alteration of the transition frequency and modal density can be observed compared to honeycomb cores. A periodic octagonal core is designed, providing up to 70 % increase of the transition frequency and a significant reduction of the modal density.

articles.title: How Much Does Auger Spectroscopy Add to XAS? A Fisher-information Analysis of Core-Hole Dynamics in Ar⁺
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26234v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) and resonant-Auger spectroscopy probe different stages of core-hole excitation and decay, but distinct spectra need not provide independent information about decay parameters. We quantify their complementarity for the Ar⁺ 2p→3d manifold using state-resolved atomic calculations and a two-parameter Fisher-information model. A common scale of primary autoionization rates s_Γ and a selective spectator-pp rescaling ηₚₚ both alter XAS linewidths. Their spectral responses are nearly collinear because the spectator-pp fraction varies weakly among populated intermediate states. We compare XAS with an effective, scan-integrated, normalized Auger spectrum defined on a final-state-energy coordinate, with fixed excitation weights and final-state widths. Within this reduced observable, the common rate scale cancels from the normalized branching fractions, while ηₚₚ redistributes intensity among ionic final states. This cancellation is a property of the adopted model, not of photon-energy-resolved resonant-Auger spectroscopy generally. Under the reference count and resolution assumptions, XAS alone yields a Cramér-Rao lower bound (CRLB) corresponding to a 1.20% local fractional standard uncertainty in the excitation-weighted total natural width; adding Auger reduces this uncertainty by only 0.70%. In contrast, the uncertainty in the spectator-pp branching fraction falls by 99.19%, with similarly large gains for partial-rate scales. A generalized Fisher comparison gives a 123.5-fold improvement on the standard-deviation scale along the most enhanced information mode. Thus, the principal benefit of the complementary Auger observable is to resolve a nearly degenerate decay-channel decomposition rather than substantially refine the total natural width.

articles.title: How Memristors Work: A Step-by-Step Guide to the CALM Model
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26273v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Memristors made of very different materials, halide perovskites, metal oxides and nanofluidic channels, show a common set of dynamical features: two limiting conductances, hysteresis that depends on the scan rate, regular and inverted hysteresis loops, large and negative capacitances and inductive loops in impedance spectra, and potentiation and depression under pulse trains. This tutorial shows how a single minimal model, the conductance-activated quasi-linear memristor (CALM) model, explains all these features with three ingredients: the two conductance states, the rectification function x_eq (u) and the characteristic time tau(u). The tutorial is a slide presentation that the reader can follow alone, with exercises designed to be solved with the help of an AI assistant, reference Python code, and this support text. The text can also be read on its own: Section 4 gives a compact account of the content of the slides, with the main equations and figures, and the solutions to the exercises are given at the end.

articles.title: Correlated detection of electrons and ions emitted from laser-induced nanoplasmas in doped helium nanodroplets in the single-shot single-cluster regime
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26280v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present single-cluster single-shot correlated measurements of electron velocity-map images and ion time-of-flight traces from individual laser-induced nanoplasmas in xenon-doped helium nanodroplets. Simultaneous detection associates the ion composition, ion kinetic energies, and electron energies with the same nanoplasma event. The detected ion composition separates events into populations dominated by He+ mono-cations versus those dominated by He²⁺ di-cations, with markedly different ion energies and electron kinetic energies. The He+-dominated population correlates well with low electron kinetic energies (< 0.5 eV), whereas the distribution of maximum electron kinetic energies for the He²⁺-dominated population shows a peak around 1 eV. Molecular dynamics simulations averaged over the focal volume suggest that local laser intensity contributes to this separation. These correlations provide single-event observables for classifying nanoplasmas and will support real-time shot-to-shot sorting in single-particle coherent diffractive imaging experiments.

articles.title: Study of non-uniformity-induced structured spectrum in a tapered optical fiber through stimulated four-wave mixing
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26282v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tapered optical fibers offer tunable dispersion and a small mode area, yielding high nonlinearity, which makes them ideal for nonlinear and quantum optics. Because phase-matched four-wave mixing strongly depends on dispersion, the taper diameter becomes a key parameter. For sub-micrometer tapers, identifying the exact diameter is challenging. Here, we show that when seeding with a broad spectrum, stimulated four-wave mixing yields a comb-like spectrum that is directly linked to the overall taper profile opening possibility for non-destructive evaluation of sub-micron taper. Our model based on joint-spectral amplitude includes the phase accumulated over the fiber length.

articles.title: Self-Oscillating Photonic Frequency Comb for Sub-THz Local Oscillator Generation in Earth Observation Systems
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26372v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Earth observation missions rely on microwave and sub-terahertz radiometry for retrieving atmospheric parameters such as temperature, humidity, and cloud properties, with the 183- and 229-GHz spectral regions being particularly relevant. Local-oscillator (LO) generation at these frequencies requires low phase noise and high frequency stability while meeting stringent size, weight, and power (SWaP) constraints. Conventional architectures employ dielectric resonator oscillators followed by cascaded frequency-multiplication stages, requiring dedicated generation chains for different frequency bands and increasing hardware complexity. Furthermore, frequency multiplication degrades the phase noise of the generated signal. This work proposes and numerically investigates a reconfigurable self-oscillating microwave photonic architecture for LO generation in Earth observation receivers. Cascaded Mach-Zehnder and phase modulation within an optoelectronic feedback loop generate an optical frequency comb with enhanced higher-order components. A combination of optical filters is used to select the required comb line. First, a conventional bandpass filter with a bandwidth of approximately 10 GHz isolates the spectral region containing the desired component, after which a narrowband dual cavity Bragg grating ring resonator (BGRR) with a bandwidth of approximately 3 MHz provides the final line selection. The selected comb line is then combined with an optical reference derived from the same laser and photodetected to generate the desired millimeter-wave or sub-terahertz signal through optical heterodyning. Numerical simulations are presented for 183- and 229-GHz generation, demonstrating the ability of the same underlying architecture to address multiple LO frequencies by tuning the OEO electrical filter to the appropriate oscillation frequency and selecting the corresponding comb order.

articles.title: A hybrid wave-mode formulation for the vibro-acoustic analysis of 2D periodic structures
articles.abstract: arXiv:2610.26386v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the framework of vibrational analysis of 2D periodic waveguides, Floquet-Bloch theorem is widely applied for the determination of wave dispersion characteristics. In this context, the Wave Finite Element Method (WFEM) combines Periodic Structure Theory (PST) with standard FE packages, enabling wave dispersion analysis of waveguides involving structurally realistic unit-cells. For such applications, the computational efficiency of the WFEM, depends on the choice of the formulation and can lead to numerical issues, worsened by extensive computational cost. This paper presents a coupled wave-mode approach for the determination of wave dispersion characteristics in structurally advanced periodic structures. It combines two scales of model order reduction. At the unit-cell's scale, Component Mode Synthesis (CMS) provides the displacement field associated with local resonances of the periodic structure, while the free wave propagation is considered using a spectral problem projection on a reduced set of shape functions associated with propagating waves, thus providing considerable reduction of the computational cost.
